Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer the question asked last Friday by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) with
regard to the employment of Indians and Eskimos on the D.E.W. line.
The arrangements made between the government of Canada and the government of the United States provide that construction contractors will be required to give preference to Canadian labour and that the rates of pay and working conditions will be set, after consultation with the Canadian Department of Labour, in accordance with the Canadian Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act. This applies to all Canadians employed including Indians and Eskimos.
Contractors are supplied by the Department of Labour with schedules establishing classifications of labour, hours of work and rates of pay for all Canadian workers employed.
Liaison between the Department of Labour and D.E.W. line contractors is maintained through a senior officer of my department at Ottawa, and all relations between the contractors and employees with respect to the observance of wage rates and hours of labour are under continual supervision by two northern service officers of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
These arrangements will also apply to the contract for the maintenance and operation of the D.E.W. line.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: D.E.W. LINE-APPLICATION OF ACT TO EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to unemployment insurance, I should like to answer the questions addressed to the Prime Minister by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar as to how unemployment insurance applies to D.E.W. line workers.
Both United States contractors and Canadian contractors engaged in the construction or maintenance of the D.E.W. line and similar projects must comply with the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act of Canada. Most of the employees who have been engaged on the construction are Canadians.
The Unemployment Insurance Act requires the contractors, whether American or Canadian, to insure their Canadian civilian employees unless they are excluded by some provision of the act such as the wage ceiling.

Inquiries of the Ministry This excludes salaried employees earning in excess of $4,800 a year. However, persons paid by the hour, by the day or at piece rates are insurable regardless of the amount of earnings.
Most of the Canadian civilian employees engaged on these projects have been brought from populated areas and the regulations provide that such persons, if normally engaged in insurable employment, continue to be insured even when transferred to remote locations in northern Canada. However, persons locally employed, if the employment is north of the 55th parallel of latitude where there are only two or three isolated industrial pockets, and if they do not ordinarily work in insurable employment but depend for their livelihood on non-insurable occupations, such as hunting and fishing, are not insurable when employed on a temporary basis on construction projects of this nature. There is only employment for a very small number of such persons, and the great bulk of the Canadian employees are insured by their employers.
All workers are covered for workmen's compensation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 23, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget brought down by the Minister of

Finance on March 20 has received throughout the country the very cool reception which it deserves. It is generally accepted by the public that this is a stand-pat budget, with the obvious intention that next year tax concessions that should have been made this year will be advanced as bait before the next general election.
That such a vitally important matter as the budget of this country should depend in such large measure on the political whims of the Liberal party is a source of deep regret.
I feel that this time next year, when the pre-election budget is brought down, the public of Canada will recognize the stratagem in deferring tax relief which we had every reason to expect should have been made this year. Then everything will be placed in its proper prospective.
I feel that there is a tendency on the part of the press and the general public to view the budget primarily in terms of adjustments made in the level of taxation. Important as that aspect may be, I think we have to recognize that the budget is the chief instrument of government policy in dealing with the pressing problems facing the country at the present time; and the worth of this budget will depend upon the ability of the government to come to grips with the problems presently facing the Canadian people.
I insist that the problems which faced parliament last year are still with us. To some extent these problems have been aggravated. One need only look at the very large segment of our population that is engaged in agriculture. We find from figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics that net farm income, which stood at $1,127 million in 1951, has declined precipitously each succeeding year and that in the last year for which full figures are available, net farm income in the prairie provinces had dropped to some $376 million. That is a decline of over 67 per cent. At the same time costs of production have increased nearly fourfold. Therefore one can readily evaluate the situation confronting agriculture in this country and can determine whether or not the government, through the budget, is alive to the situation and prepared to undertake measures to bring about a reversal of this dangerous trend.
Then, of course, we have the question of unemployment. I suppose the government feels that there no longer is a problem in Canada because there are only a little over half a million people looking for employment, whereas last year the figure went a little higher. Hon. members will recall that when we discussed the question of unemployment last year it appeared quite obvious that the government was willing to accept as natural
The Budget-Mr. Ellis a very large degree of unemployment. Economists tell us that in a free labour market there will be at any given time a small group of people who are changing jobs or who, at a given time, are looking for employment. But at no time should that number exceed 2 per cent or at the most 3 per cent of the labour force, and any time unemployment figures exceed that percentage we are faced not with frictional unemployment of a regional or seasonal nature but with general unemployment.
If the government feel they can take satisfaction from the fact that this year the number of jobless rose only to 515,000, then in my opinion they are indicating a most callous disregard for this major problem. I ask all members of the house to view the budget objectively and in conjunction with any other legislation proposed by the government this year, and ask themselves whether the government is doing anything toward the solution of these two basic problems, the question of declining farm income on the one hand and widespread unemployment on the other.
It is the custom of government apologists to rationalize unemployment by suggesting that because it is regional or seasonal there is nothing that can be done about it. I question the validity of that argument. In a country such as Canada we are naturally going to be faced with the problem of regional and seasonal unemployment, and that is all the more reason the government should be taking appropriate steps to meet the situation. When we find in many parts of Canada distressed areas because of the closing down of industry, then it is the responsibility of the government to do something through a public investment program to provide alternative employment. The government cannot argue that seasonal or regional unemployment is like the weather and nothing can be done about it. Indeed, the solution of frictional unemployment in this country is of major concern to all thinking people, and it ought to be part and parcel of an over-all government policy aimed at eliminating unemployment in this country.
I think Canadians generally accept the principle that there is no reason for unemployment in the country and that full employment should be made the conscious effort of government policy. Yet what is the situation? It is far removed from the years that immediately followed world war II, when the government had enough bold plans for providing full employment, and when they had this shelf of public works that was going to be brought into being immediately unemployment became of serious consequence. We find that was just so much

The Budget-Mr. Ellis window dressing, so much talk to be conveniently trotted out before a general election and immediately forgotten when the smoke of electoral battle cleared away.
We in the C.C.F. movement recognize the need for action in these fields. I want to suggest that, in looking at the budget objectively, we must consider it in relation to the economic difficulties facing the country at the present time. Then there is another aspect to which we must give careful consideration, and that is the question of our whole tax structure. It is not my intention to deal in any detail with this matter. Our leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, dealt very ably with this matter in his address a week ago. At that time he pointed out the most glaring inequities in our tax structure.
Specifically I believe some mention was made of dividend credits. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out in this house that so unfair and so iniquitous is our tax structure that a married man with no children and earning $3,000 a year is required to pay $150 in income tax, yet a man could be making $14,000 and pay only $60. He could be getting $14,000 in dividends and be required to pay only the social security portion of the income tax, namely $60. There is something wrong with a tax structure that permits those who derive their income from dividends on invested capital to get off virtually scot free while the man with a low income who earns his money is required to pay income tax. I think it is generally agreed that originally the income tax was intended as a device to tax the wealthy, but over the years there has been a tendency to reduce the level at which income tax is to be paid, so that today many families who actually are able to do no more than provide the necessities of life are required to pay income tax.
Another inequity of the tax structure had to do with depletion allowances. Here again there are tax concessions to those who could well afford to make a fair contribution to the public purse. Then of course there is the question of capital gains. Here is a field in which the reluctance or the refusal of this government to give some consideration to requiring Canadians who make money through capital gains to make their fair contribution to the tax coffers of this country indicates where the sympathies of this government lie. Certainly they are not with the low income group. They are very interested to go out of their way to extend tax concessions and to do everything within their power to assist those who are well able to look after themselves, while they consistently refuse to grant the type of tax relief which will benefit the small man in this country.


We in this group recognize that there is great need for an increase in the exemption levels which have existed over the years. We have insisted that there should be an increase of $1,000 in the income tax exemption levels for both single and married people. While we advocate that, we recognize that the only way you are going to bring about a measure of tax relief to a great percentage of the people of Canada is through a reduction in the sales and excise taxes. In spite of all the glowing talk of government apologists about the prosperous times in this country, let us not forget that there are many families throughout Canada that have never earned sufficient money to be required to pay any income tax at all. If you are to be fair, if you are to be just and give tax relief where it is needed the most, then you will have to do something about reducing the sales and excise taxes.
As far as capital gains are concerned, I was particularly interested last year in reading a little account in the U. S. News and World Report, indicating the part that capital gains play in the building up of great fortunes. They give a very good example. Executives of certain corporations there in April of 1951 had an option to buy 5,000 shares of stock at $99 a share. The option to purchase expired in five years if not exercised. In May of the same year the corporation split its stock two shares for one. Those directors could now buy 10,000 shares of stock at $49.50 a share. That was the price of the stock split. In January of 1953 the price went up to $67.38 per share. The directors took up the option to buy 10,000 shares at $49.50 a share. On a total price of $495,000 the paper profit realized in this instance was $178,800. In May of 1954 the stock went up to $129 a share and the corporation split the shares again two for one. The stock was now worth $64.50 a share and the 20,000 shares in existence had a total value of $1,290,000, and the profit was $795,000. Then in February, 1955, the market price of the stock was $132.50. The directors sold 20,000 shares at this price and received $2,650,000. This constituted a profit of $2,155,000. In the United States they have a capital gains tax of 25 per cent. Therefore the director paid his tax of $538,750 and ended up with a clear profit of $1,616,250.
The same pattern is true in this country. The only difference is that in this country there is no capital gains tax. In other words, they actually do better in these monopolies in Canada because of the absence of this very necessary form of taxation, yet

the government will hold the line in tax concessions. There are no reductions in sales tax, but at the same time the government refuses to place a proper share of the burden on the backs of those who are well able to take that responsibility.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, we have to look at this budget from the standpoint of the general tax structure. If we do that we will not be satisfied waiting for another year when the Minister of Finance will come out just before the next election and offer us a little bit of a tax concession. What we need is a revamping of our tax structure in order that those who are better able to bear the burden will be called upon to pay a proper share.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are one or two comments I should like to make about the unemployment situation. I referred briefly to the need for a public investment program, because if we are to rely upon private enterprise to do it we will wait a long time. I think the resolution now before the house having to do with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is a specific instance where private capital refused to do the job and we were forced into the humiliating position of having to go outside this country for capital. The obvious answer in that instance would be public investment, a publicly-owned pipe line. There are many projects in this country which could be undertaken at the present time which would add to the productive capacity of Canada, which would add to our material wealth and which would build up the country. These could only be done through a proper program of public investment.
In my own province we have had frequent reference to the South Saskatchewan river dam. It has been made a political football by the Liberal party. They throw it out before elections time after time in an effort to win votes, and they have played both ends against the middle. A year ago they said the province of Saskatchewan was not prepared to pay enough, and I think last year the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) said he thought the province was paying too much.
Figures were produced last year as to the cost of this project. The Minister of Agriculture now suggests that these figures are too high. He has indicated that he knows people who will do the job for $83 million. I suggest that he should take the house into his confidence and let us know who these people are, because if the job could be done for that amount I see no reason why there could not be an immediate agreement to go ahead with this project at the present time.
The Budget-Mr. Ellis
I realize, of course, that various opinions have been expressed in the province of Saskatchewan by supporters of this government in Ottawa. The leader of the Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan has been going about the province making speeches. It has been his practice to pass off the dam as being of no consequence while speaking in one area, and in the next place he suggests that he is all in favour of it. He made an extremely significant statement, however, when he said that "we will never get the dam until we kick this government out of here", meaning the provincial government. When I suggest that this measure has been used as a political football by the Liberal party I think there is ample evidence to back up my statement.
I believe there are many other fields in which the federal government ought to be taking action in order to develop this country. Many of the provinces would prefer to go ahead and develop their resources but they lack the fiscal power to do the job. There is no doubt that the people in the province of Saskatchewan find themselves in that position. We want to develop our resources, but the province does not have the fiscal power. We are not unique in this respect, because no province has the necessary financial power to do a large-scale job of public investment; consequently, as second best, it is necessary to rely on outside capital. The fault lies not with the provinces, whether it be the province of British Columbia or any other province in Canada. The responsibility lies squarely on the shoulders of the government in Ottawa.
There are one or two other matters I would like to raise at this time. I want to make reference now to a matter which has attracted my attention since coming into this house. The growth of the trade union movement in Canada has of course brought about a new concept in employer-employee relationships. The old concept of master and servant has been replaced by collective bargaining between management and labour. No longer is the employee in organized industry in constant fear of unfair treatment or unjust dismissal. As a member of his union working with his fellows in the union he is able to meet with management and evolve a satisfactory working agreement mutually acceptable to both sides governing such matters as wages, hours of work, holidays, seniority, grievance procedure and all the other matters that have vexed relationships between management and labour. As a result labour has become a partner in industry, in large measure, and is working more efficiently in the industrial field.
In spite of the fact that in the early days employers fought tooth and nail to halt the

The Budget-Mr. Ellis growth ot the trade union movement, and despite the fact that some still resist it, many enlightened employers realize that unions are here to stay and collective bargaining procedures are always going to be with us. The unfortunate thing is that there are large groups of Canadian employees who are denied the rights of collective bargaining. I say they are rights because they are rights which are guaranteed by law in many instances. I believe union recognition has become more than just a sanction on the part of an employer who has to deal with the rights of the employees in his plant. Collective bargaining has been sanctioned by law in Canada.
Well, what about the civil servants? I take pride in the fact that the province of Saskatchewan is the only province in Canada which permits proper collective bargaining procedure for civil servants.

speechtext: Oh, you are crazy.

speechtext: I hear a dissenting voice on my left. The Canadian council of public employee associations held a meeting in Regina-

speechtext: Where is that?

speechtext:
-about a year and a half ago. As I pointed out, this organization represents some 40,000 public servants, employees of provincial governments, including the provincial governments of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario. The council passed the following resolution:
Whereas provincial public servants in all provinces of Canada, except Saskatchewan, have no negotiation, conciliation or arbitration rights in dealing with their employers, and
Whereas, we believe this condition to be a negation of democratic principles and a denial of the right granted by law to other organized bodies of the working society,
Therefore, be it resolved that this council go on record approving in principle of the belief that negotiation, conciliation and arbitration rights be granted by provincial governments to their employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask my hon. friend to repeat the name of the organization?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is the Canadian council of public employee associations. This resolution was passed on August 30, 1954.
I mentioned the fact that the provincial governments were mentioned in their resolution. This was because at that time only


provincial representatives were in attendance, and they did not go beyond making recommendations to their own governments. However, the same principle is involved in relation to the federal government. There is no reason why federal civil servants should be denied collective bargaining rights.
In my own province we placed no obstacles in the way of collecting bargaining procedures, and we also were willing and anxious to treat our public servants in the province in the same way we expect any decent employer in the country to treat his employees.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then would you explain its application to the bus drivers in Saskatchewan?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is asking a question which I think he might more properly elaborate into a speech a little later on. I suggest that when the province of British Columbia gets around to granting collective bargaining rights for provincial civil servants the hon. member will then have a reason for making an interjection of that kind. In the meantime I suggest that you put pressure on the Social Credit government in British Columbia to do the decent thing for their public servants by granting them collective bargaining rights.
We in this group are in the position of being able to come before this house and make our point quite clear, because we have done what we have preached in this house. We have granted to our public servants full collective bargaining rights. We suggest that what has been done in our province can be done in every other province in this country, and can be done here in Ottawa by the federal government. It ill behooves anyone from a province with an anti-labour government like the Social Credit government in British Columbia to make absurd interjections like that.
The only way we are going to bring about more co-operation with and a better spirit among our public servants is to grant them collective bargaining rights. I hear these frequent interjections, and I realize that I have touched on a sore spot as far as the Social Crediters are concerned. Of course their anti-labour policies are known from one end of this country to the other. They are trying to out-Tory the Tories in their antilabour policy. This is self-evident and needs no elaboration by me at the present time.
I am suggesting that the government could avoid many of the difficulties which it now encounters when dealing with its public servants if it agreed with the employee organizations to sit around a table in a proper

spirit of collective bargaining in an effort to arrive at a settlement and wage contract which would be mutually acceptable to both sides. We would then have something in the nature of proper employee-employer relationship in this country.
There is one reference I should like to make to the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance, in connection with housing. The minister pointed out that in the last year there had been an increase in residential construction, and that perhaps for the first time we had reached the stage where home construction was keeping pace with or perhaps staying a little in advance of new family units in Canada.
The main problem in so far as housing in this country is concerned still remains unsolved. There are over half a million homes in this country which are certainly in need of replacement. Pardon me, I should not say replacement; according to the brief presented to the government by the Canadian Congress of Labour a year ago there were some half million dwellings needed to meet the backlog of housing requirements in Canada.
What steps have been taken by the government to meet this great backlog? We know that the population of Canada is growing, and that the new homes which the Minister of Finance talked about are needed to keep pace with that growing population. But we still face a tremendous backlog of housing need in Canada. Beyond the need for new residential construction is a great need for homes to replace older homes, many unfit for human habitation, and many in such a condition as to create a hazard, particularly with regard to fires. I think the government should take these factors into consideration.
There are almost 1,000,000 homes in Canada now overcrowded or in need of major repairs; there are some 900,000 homes with no inside running water, and almost 1,500,000 homes with no bath or shower facilities for exclusive family use. There are over 1,200,000 homes with no flush toilets; nearly 600,000 with no hot water supply; over 1,700,000 with no electric or gas stoves; 1,757,000 with no mechanical refrigeration, and over 1,700,000 without furnaces.
Think of what these needs mean in terms of jobs, when we have an unemployment situation in Canada. There is no lack of work to be done, in fact there is a vast amount of work to be done. Then we should think also in terms of the danger to human life that exists in many of these dwellings.
In recent months we have been shocked by the tragic fires which have occurred in the
The Budget-Mr. Ellis Ottawa district and throughout Canada. The death toll this year has been shocking. I think it was on March 16 that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked tbe Prime Minister whether he would not consider taking the initiative in doing something to bring an end to these tragic fires. As usual, the Prime Minister shrugged off the responsibility and said this was purely a matter for the provinces. I suggest that it is not a matter purely for the provinces. I speak only from my reading of press reports, from seeing pictures were published, but these indicate that many of these homes which were destroyed were substandard. The inquest reports and reports of inquiries that have been held almost invariably indicate that the dwellings were substandard. We are told that in many cases the walls were nothing more than pressed paper. Once a fire started there was little or no hope of the occupants escaping. Is it any wonder that we have had such an appalling loss of human life, particularly of children who have perished this winter in fires right here in the Ottawa area?
What is the answer? Apart from the precautions which an individual must take at all times, the answer seems to be to do something about the substandard housing that exists in this country. As long as people are required to live in houses that are mere shells with partitions made of pressed paper, we cannot expect to avoid tragic fires like these. If the federal government are anxious and willing to do something about this great problem they should start by doing something in the field of public housing over and above what is done under the National Housing Act.
As far as the National Housing Act is concerned, hon. members will recall that when the amended act was brought down in 1954 we of the C.C.F. group had certain criticisms to offer. We pointed out that the legislation would not assist the people of Canada who needed help, that is those in the very low income groups. We pointed out that the interest rate was excessive, particularly when the lending institutions, the banks, were having their loans guaranteed at the borrower's expense. There was a guarantee that there would be no loss to the banks.
Under those circumstances there seemed to be no fair relationship between the risk involved and the interest rate charged, as the banks were taking no risk whatsoever. There seemed to be no justification for the interest rate provided in the legislation. Sinct

The Budget-Mr. Ellis that time the government has seen fit to increase the interest rate still more.
We pointed out at the time that housing needs in Canada were such that the National Housing Act would be powerless to deal with the basic problem. What has happened since?
I have here a table based on Canadian housing statistics for the third quarter of 1955, published by Central Mortgage and Housing
Corporation, and I should like to have unanimous consent to place this on Hansard.

the fact that over the years there has been a marked increase in the use of N.H.A. loans by those in the higher income groups, and there has been a gradual tapering off of borrowers in the lower income groups, so that they are almost negligible. As a matter of fact, home-owner borrowers with gross family incomes below $3,500 comprised only 4-1 per cent of total borrowers under N.H.A. in 1954. By mid-1955 this percentage figure had dropped to 3 per cent. That bears out the points we made at that time, that the National Housing Act, however it may assist a small group in the country, has failed to meet the needs of people earning less than $3,500 a year. They are the people who are forced to live in these substandard homes of which I spoke a moment ago.
The government cannot feel that the National Housing Act is meeting the problem. What we need at the present time is a housing program that will be tailored to meet the needs of the people who need the housing most. We have a tragic situation where so many of our people unable to raise the money for the down payment are paying rents greatly in excess of what they would have o pay in payments on homes. I received letter the other day from a constituent who [Mr. Ellis. 1

payment he would only have to make monthly payments of $72 on a house; but he could not raise the down payment. In the meantime he is paying over $100 in rent, and he cannot save any money as long as he must go on paying rent.
Something must be done by this government to provide for the housing needs of these low income groups. In many instances, of course, owing to the transitory nature of their employment, low rental housing would have to be provided for some people. In any event the time has come when the government should give serious consideration to revamping its housing program to provide for the needs of low income groups in this country.
I know my time is fleeting, Mr. Speaker, but before I sit down I want to make some reference to a very important matter. I am sure all hon. members were disappointed and shocked the other day at the news that another atomic test had been held within the Soviet union. I am sure thinking people throughout the world will deplore this madness in persisting in experimenting with these horrific weapons. Members of this group have drawn this matter to the attention of the house on former occasions, pointing out that

the risks involved are not commensurate with any foreseeable advantages to be gained.
Surely we have gone far enough in this field. No one can say with absolute certainty the effects these experiments are going to have on the human race. Many scientists are very apprehensive about the genetic and other effects on human beings. There may be those who will disclaim any ill effects from these particular experiments, but I suggest, whether these experiments are conducted, as the most recent ones were, by the Soviet union, or by the United States or by Great Britain, this parliament ought to make its wishes known and make the strongest representations to the governments concerned, asking them on behalf of the Canadian people to cease forthwith any further tests of this type.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very remiss indeed in my duty, coming from a border riding, if I did not say at the very outset a few words pertaining to the visit of our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) with the President of the United States, Mr. Eisenhower. At Niagara Falls we pride ourselves on the rainbow which is visible at most times of the day and which is a connecting link, and indeed a symbol of friendship and peace, between two great countries and two great friends. Certainly the visit of our Prime Minister and his external affairs minister with the President of the United States is a symbolization of those characteristics that we in Canada wish to extend to the great United States; peace and friendship. I know we all wish the Prime Minister well in his visit.
Contrary to what was said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I want to compliment the government, and indeed the Minister of Labour, for doing their utmost to maintain full employment as far as possible. It is my firm belief that the people of Canada have the ability, the courage, the determination and the ambition to produce on their farms and in their factories, as far as possible, increased quantities of goods and services for ever-increasing numbers of people.
Many people have asked, and rightly so, what does it take to make a job? In the first place it takes a man or woman who cannot be employed unless people are willing to buy the thing he or she produces or unless people need his or her services. So jobs and manufacturing are the end result of a number of things. Before there can be a manufacturing job there must be an idea for a product that people want, and there must be people
The Budget-Mr. Houck willing to risk their savings in furnishing capital to develop that idea. Then before there can be a job there must be customers. When a customer buys a product, the money he spends creates work; work for the people in the plants; work for those who supply raw materials; work for those who sell and service that product.
In the end it is the customer who makes the job. It is by careful estimates of the number of customers that management is able to plan that work and the number of jobs that will be created. To begin with, someone or some group of people must have sufficient confidence in the products, in the requirement for services of one form or another, and sufficient confidence in the people who are going to manufacture and market those products or who will be providing the various services, to risk their savings in financing the undertaking. Money must be provided for plants and machinery. This amounts to a considerable sum for every job. Everyone who has savings at work expects some return for their use. Therefore, in order that jobs may be created and may continue to exist, there must be a chance to make a reasonable profit.
So, to sum up, jobs are the end result of something; the result of a combination of capital, management and opportunity, with some catalyst thrown in to make them fuse and function. This fourth factor, however, can hardly be described in one word. Its foundation, of course, is confidence and belief in the future of enterprise that is established by sound national and economic policies.
Manufacturing as a whole provides over one and a half million jobs in Canada today. Of this total the automotive manufacturing concerns absorb a little over 350,000 men- in short, about one job in every 15 jobs in the country. This does not include, of course, garages, service stations or supplies such as steel mills, manufacturers of textiles, tires, etc. Last year in this debate I referred to the tax on automobiles, and I was in hopes that something would be done in this regard to make it easier and cheaper for the average man to buy his much needed motor car. I thought this would tend also to increase the business of the automobile manufacturers.
The outlook for the motor car business is excellent for many years to come because of the vast economic expansion we are undergoing, and the job of building cars and trucks will be a major industrial item in Canada for an indefinite period to come. Judging from the fact that this is a big business and that there are over 4,000 automobile dealers in Canada, over 14,000 independent garages and over 16,000 service stations throughout
2644	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Houck our great dominion, it is quite obvious that the sale and servicing of motor vehicles offers employment in a wide field of occupations.
I should like to say that there are countless opportunities not only in the automotive business but in industry as well for every man and woman in this country who wants to make a go of it. We as Canadians have the qualities that make for greatness. These qualities are obvious to anyone who has studied the characteristics of the people who go to make up this great nation. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that last year's records will show that when the tax on automobiles was reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent it resulted in increased business, increased sales and thereby an increase in tax revenue.
I am still of the opinion that this tax is not only a special tax but that it is unfair, unjust and economically unsound. I say that if this tax could be removed it would help materially to stimulate sales and would thereby certainly maintain more production and more employment. This is not a one-way street as far as this subject is concerned, and I do not think people should expect the government to go all the way. I think the average car buyer realizes, thinks and believes, and rightly so, that the automobile manufacturer must go part of the way. Therefore I believe that if the government and the automobile manufacturer would each go part of the way it would be a lot easier for the average man to own a motor car, and to buy it within the resources of his pocketbook.
I am anxious that the Minister of Finance give consideration to the paying of taxes on all federal buildings and land. The reduction from 4 per cent to 2 per cent passed at the last session was to broaden the scope of the grants so that a greater number of municipalities might qualify. I think the two main factors in the legislation are that the percentage factor was reduced from 4 per cent to 2 per cent, and the legislation did liberalize the formula to increase the payments by relating the grant to the ratio of federal property to taxable property only, instead of the ratio of federal property to taxable and federal property combined. This, of course, removes the 75 per cent factor, so that the combined effect would be to calculate the grants at the full real property tax rate.
I felt that this bill indicated that the government recognized the fact that municipalities were entitled to taxation revenue. If this is true, Mr. Speaker, I say why not full taxation? Why not go all the way? I cannot understand why special treatment should be given to crown agencies, and in saying that I include not only federal but provincial agencies as well, since all too frequently these


agencies are engaged in activities that are definitely in competition with private agencies which, of course, must of necessity pay the full amount of taxation levied in the area in which they operate.
You cannot overlook the fact, Mr. Speaker, that federal and provincial properties are entitled to and receive exactly the same services as any other property but pay nothing toward their cost. Ninety-nine times out of 100 the federal or provincial building is situated on one of the choicest locations in the municipality and immediately it is taken out of taxation, thus reducing the potential revenue of the municipality. To supply the necessary services I have just mentioned the municipalities' prime source of revenue is the taxpayer, and certainly everyone must agree that the ratepayer can stand no further demands upon his finances.
The Municipal Grants Act amendment may sound very good in the press but I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that as far as the city of Niagara Falls and the township of Stanford are concerned, both of which I am extremely proud of and both of which are known the world over, it does not mean a thing. The federal assessment in the city of Niagara Falls, although a very sizeable sum, does not come within the required percentage to entitle that city to any grant. In Niagara Falls alone we have well over $700,000 of federal exempt assessment out of a total of some $16 million exempt assessment. I admit that of this total exemption the province has the lion's share, approximately $12,500,000, but as far as federal property is concerned nothing is received by way of federal aid.
May I crave the patience and indulgence of hon. members of the house, Mr. Speaker, to cite a case in point pertaining to the city of Niagara Falls. The loss to the city by receiving a grant from the Ontario hydro in lieu of taxes last year was almost $250,000. This was clearly shown by a study of the assessment roll. This loss has steadily increased during the last few years as the value of both hydro and other properties has increased with the grant at the same time remaining almost at a stationary level.
At the present time the city of Niagara Falls and the township of Stamford each receives the sum of $75,000 as a grant in lieu of taxes. This grant has been in vogue for many years and it does not seem fair, in view of the increase in property value and the fact that the value of our dollar has gone down, that we should have to suffer such a loss. In Niagara Falls and Stamford we simply have to face it. Through no fault of their own both these places are in a very

poor position from the standpoint of assessment value. If I might mention it in passing, the Rainbow bridge only pays the sum of $12,000 per annum in lieu of taxation. This amount was based on the assessment away back in the early forties, and Niagara Falls is dropping thousands of dollars a year in that respect.
This does not seem fair to me when the Peace bridge, which occupies almost the same amount of land as the bridge at Niagara Falls, pays to the municipality of Fort Erie- and I am very happy that it does-the sum of $40,000 a year, which will be increased by an escalator clause to $60,000 a year in the year 1962. We have a case in point of the stores under the Rainbow bridge which are controlled by the department of highways of the province of Ontario. When the stores were erected the provincial government agreed to pay the city of Niagara Falls $8,000 a year in lieu of taxation. That has continued for some years, but the city was notified by the provincial minister concerned that at the end of 1955 this sum would cease to be paid.
In comparison with the sum of $75,000 a year paid to Niagara Falls and the township of Stamford, may I say that even in the year 1953 the Canadian Niagara Power Company paid in taxes to the township of Stamford over $288,000. This plant is only rated at 100,000 horsepower, compared with the terrific amount of horsepower developed by the hydro plants.
We in Niagara Falls are very happy to have these government employees. We have over 400 federal government employees and about 850 men and women working for the power commission. We are very proud of them. They are making exceptionally fine citizens and are heartily welcome in our city. But we definitely feel that from both the federal and provincial governments we should receive some compensation for the services we have to provide. I want to say here that the premier of Ontario is continually crying to high heaven for more aid from Ottawa. Everybody knows that the municipalities are the prime responsibility of the provincial government, and I submit to the premier of the province of Ontario that he should practice what he preaches and see to it that the municipalities receive the much-needed aid they so justly deserve.
I would not want to let this opportunity go by without at least saying a word about the civil servants I have in my riding. Probably no other member of the house has more immigration and customs officials in his riding. They are the first official greeters of visitors to this great Dominion of Canada and
The Budget-Mr. Houck are doing a splendid job. They are ambassadors of friendship. I have had many tourists tell me when they come across one of the bridges that their first welcome to Canada was the one they appreciated most, and how complimentary and courteous these officers were at the various ports of entry.
I think we as members and supporters of this government can look with pride upon these officers. They are great ambassadors of friendship. I only hope that when the announcement is made pertaining to civil servants' pay, these men's services will be adequately recognized. I want to say to the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that they can be exceptionally proud of these officials.
The reaction of the Canadian people to the budget I think has been one of acceptance and, if I may use a slang expression, of "father knows best". There is a deep and abiding confidence in those charged with responsibility of office never heretofore exhibited. Some have called it a stand-pat budget. I should like to call it a "don't rock the boat" budget. There is much to stand pat about, Mr. Speaker, because employment was never higher, corporation profits were never higher, personal income was never higher and the outlook for the future was never better. Hence, Mr. Speaker, I say this. Why fiddle when Rome is not burning?
There are two great national undertakings in the wings but not yet fully on the scene. I refer to the national pipe line and health insurance. The first will make greater use of our natural resources by Canadians. The second will preserve, maintain and improve our human resources. Both undertakings are imaginative in scope, and the Canadian people can anticipate with confidence that they will benefit from both.
I think it is worthy of note that there has been no general outcry against the budget. This does not usually happen when there are no direct tax reductions. I believe it is well to read the signs. So great is the confidence of the people in this government and its monetary and fiscal policies that they are prepared to let the government deal with these matters in the way it thinks best. This deep and abiding faith has come from years of benefit derived from policies bold and courageous. Last year we budgeted for a deficit. It was unusual, yet it was accepted. This year we have budgeted for a surplus, and that is even more welcome.
I cannot help feeling, as I am quite confident the majority of the people of the dominion feel, that the economic policy of this government has been well tested and has

The Budget-Mr. Houck not been found wanting. I quite well recall that in his speech last year, as recorded at page 2733 of Hansard of 1955, the Minister of Finance said this:
I propose to recommend to the house a tax policy and a tax structure that would produce a balanced budget under conditions which represent a high level of output and employment.
This indeed was a very definite answer from the government to those critics who were predicting nothing more or less than blue ruin for our country. I feel that this government has offered the country a policy that not only acts as a safeguard but indeed is a splendid example to take us through the minor ups and downs of our economy. Many condemned the budget of last year. Some said that it did hardly anything. Some said that it did not do a thing. Some said that it did not go far enough. Some said it was too conscientious.
The budget last year was the same as that which was presented by the Minister of Finance a few nights ago, and was based on sound principles and sound business ethics. The budget of last year did everything that could be expected of it; and surely, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance was sticking to the same principles of budgeting which guided us so successfully through last year and which guided him so successfully through his difficulties of last year, we shall again obtain fine results from this budget.
There is no doubt in my mind that Canada has growing pains, and I hope these growing pains will increase. Certainly the people of this dominion, with their confidence in this government and in the Minister of Finance, realize that this is going to be one of the finest years in the history of Canada. I wonder if anyone else could have presented a different budget under these circumstances. We must realize that next year we face large expenditures not only because of the new federal-provincial tax plan but because of the prospect of the hospital insurance plan which I spoke about a few minutes ago. If I may use a vernacular expression, Mr. Speaker, I would say that when everything is going all right there is no use in upsetting the applecart.
It seems to me that at a time like this, when we are receiving bad news from various parts of the world, it was encouraging to me at least to hear the Minister of Finance predict a good year ahead of us. With employment and production at high and satisfactory rates, I think the minister rightly believes that the government, business and the people of Canada must combine in perfect harmony to ensure continued prosperity, and he expresses the hope to the people that we
[Mr. Houck.3

shall have a steady increase in business rather than an immediate upward thrust.
The imagination of the Canadian people brought this country to this wonderful full development we are enjoying, and there is no reason to believe that we cannot go ahead under these circumstances, when we have a government that offers these safeguards against any monopolistic or other practices that would prove harmful to our great dominion. We in Canada are talking today in terms of 15 million people. I think in the not too distant future we shall be talking in terms of at least 30 million people. What we need is greater faith, wider vision and indeed that thing called ambition to go ahead with the job and see to it that this country is fully developed. I think we should thank almighty God that we here in Canada have a marvellous country, a marvellous future and almost incredible potential wealth.
So I say to the Minister of Finance and to the government that our resources are sound. Those men who are elected to look after the finances and the economy of our government I know will be tested as statesmen and not found wanting. I know the many requests that are made to them and the many things they hear, but 1 know they will not adhere to any of these patent medicine ideas. I want to say to the minister-and I say this to the people as well-that as long as we have faith in ourselves, in our heritage and in our destiny, Canada will be one of the greatest countries in the world in the not too distant future.
If I might use the parlance of the baseball field I say to the Minister of Finance that just a few nights ago, in presenting his budget, he had three men on bases and although the ball did not go quite over the fence, it reached the top of the fence and bounced back into the playing field. However, the bases were cleared. I am sure that next year, when our great Minister of Finance brings down his budget, he will come up again with three men on the bases and the ball will go over the fence for a home run. I want to say to him and through him to the government on behalf of everyone in the riding that I have the honour to represent, that we are proud of you. Carry on, and we are behind you to a man.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many members in this house last Tuesday evening wondered what the Minister of Finance was doing on that occasion. My friend the hon. member for Niagara Falls has now supplied the answer. The minister was apparently engaged in a baseball game, some kind of sport. He certainly was not engaged in the serious business of responsible budget-making.

"The budget is not merely dull; it is defeatist. It is not merely stand-pat; it is negative. It reads as if the minister and the Department of Finance have thrown in their hands and stopped trying. No line of policy is followed to its logical conclusion. There is nothing coherent and constructive. It is fair to say that the nearest the minister got to a policy was a sort of resigned nod to the spending departments of government to go ahead and spend".
Those are not my words. Those are words that ought to be quoted in this house. They come from the Winnipeg Free Press, and will supply an effective answer to the hon. member for Niagara Falls and others like-minded who undertake to tell this house that the Canadian people have accepted the budget, and that father knows best. That attitude, of course, is one that has become typical in this house of supporters of the government. "Father knows best". You see the category in which members taking that attitude put themselves. They are the children. Father knows best and these children, as they regard themselves, are simply to follow and toe the party line.
Well, sir, it is in no personal sense that I must say to the Minister of Finance, in referring to the budget effort on this occasion, that it was unquestionably the worst failure in Canadian history within living memory. In kitchen terms this budget is as dull as dishwater, and it fell as flat as a pancake. At the outset of the budget someone should have called from the chair or elsewhere "dispense". At the outset this speech could just as easily have been dispensed with. Indeed, sir, if this represents the government's idea of a budget it might just as well have been dispensed with entirely. It might have been better for the government simply to announce that it was not bringing down a budget this year.
What is its purpose? What is its pattern? What is the thought behind it? What are the governing considerations? Sir, these are so muddled as to be utterly incomprehensible.
Nevertheless, there was one thing .the budget did contain. It ended up with praise of the Prime Minister. Well, one can see perhaps some purpose in that. It is about the only thing one can find in the budget that has purpose and pattern to it. One recalls the words of the poet:
-praise, that last infirmity of noble minds.
One of Lord Lyttleton's poems puts it this way, Mr. Speaker:
There is no weapon that slays
Its victim so surely, if well aimed, as praise.
What was the purpose of this praise? It may possibly have been to coax the Prime Minister down from the remote fence on
The Budget-Mr. Fleming which he has sat during this session, to try to stir up in him some interest in the affairs of parliament, an interest which he has not indicated in any shape or form throughout this session. What may have been the purpose may well be left to speculation. But the Prime Minister is still on the side lines. He still takes his remote, detached place, with little or no interest in the house.
Now, sir, if I refer to this document and its proposals as a budget, let me enter the reservation that I do so in name only. This is not a budget in the proper sense of the word, but I will call it a budget because that is the most convenient way of referring to it.
The first feature of this budget, sir, is that it proposes to exact an increased tax levy from the Canadian people. The tax imposition is by the government's proposals to be raised to an all-time record height, $4,763 million. This aspect of the budget has of course been covered up very subtly with a multitude of words; but it is a fact that the government proposes to take out of the pockets of the people $378 million more this coming year than it took out of those same pockets during the past year. It proposes to take something over $1 million a day out of the pockets of the Canadian people more than it took last year. That, sir, is a sum far exceeding the rate of increase in the population of this country. It means, sir, an increase of $23.62 per capita in the dominion tax levies.
The second question of interest that one can apply to this budget is, what bearing has it on inflation? The budget is extremely vague on this subject. I should be inclined to question whether this factor entered into the considerations of the government at all. The minister talks about the "renewal of inflationary pressures in many countries". He speaks of the operations of the Bank of Canada "directed increasingly toward moderating the rate of expansion in the use of credit", and then he allows himself, apparently, to relate this to some aspects of government responsibility; for the minister says at page 2327 of Hansard:
The federal government itself has a special responsibility to see that its fiscal policies continue to be directed towards economic stability. The use of the flexible instruments of monetary policy is also being directed towards this objective.
Well, sir, that was very little indeed to say in a budget speech by way of review of some facts and events that have occurred within the year. The fact is the Bank of Canada lowered the bank rate from 2 per cent to 1J per cent on February 1. On August 5 it reversed the policy and raised the bank rate from 1J per cent back to 2 per cent. On October 12 it raised it from 2 per cent to 2\ per cent; and on November 18, from
2648	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fleming 2| per cent to 2| per cent. The policy has been confusing to say the least. If action of this kind was required, it was required before it was taken. The effects of this series of sudden increases in the bank rate have been disturbing to confidence. Every time the bank rate was raised it had the effect of subtracting millions of dollars from the value of bonds held by Canadians, including dominion government bonds.
We should like to know, and surely this house is entitled to know, what is the government's purpose in this matter? How serious is the view they take of the way inflationary forces are working? What is to be the scope of anti-inflationary policy? Give us something to judge their efforts by. Mr. James Muir, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, in his annual speech said this on inflation, a few days ago:
Experience shows that monetary policy is more effective against inflation than against deflation. But there are dangers. As I have already pointed out, the policy may go too far. It may also be unselective, curbing healthy as well as unhealthy or excessive bank credit.
What is the government's next step, sir? The government has not told us whether it regards inflation as serious or not. The minister has talked about the stability in the cost of living. That does not seem to suggest that the government thinks there is inflation; and yet we have a series of three increases in the bank discount rate. Well, if the government has any clear thinking on this matter, Mr. Speaker, we should have had some statement on it and some expression of objective.
While the minister was laying down that role with respect to what he calls the flexible instruments of monetary policy, he did not stop there; he went on to read this lecture to individual Canadians:
But careful judgment and wise spending policies are not solely matters of concern to public authorities. They are the normal responsibility of each one of us, regardless of his role in the economy.
I do not quarrel with that as a statement, but I ask the government to apply its own medicine to itself. When it is busy prescribing for individual Canadians I say, "Physician, heal thyself". The greatest inflationary pressure that exists today is reckless government expenditure and extravagance. And, sir, if the government is going to preach the virtues of thrift and care to the individual Canadian, I say let it begin in its own house. While plucking the mote from the eye of the individual Canadian, I say to the government "first pluck the beam out


of thine own eye". There is no more inflationary force in Canada today than the full weight of reckless government expenditure and extravagance.
The next matter to be mentioned, sir, is the income tax. It is true that the rate is unchanged. It should have been reduced. Of course, we are going to have to wait until election year for those increases in the exemptions which are long overdue. It is interesting to see that the C.C.F. in their amendment have sought to urge a reduction in the burden of income tax on the lower income groups. Well, in 1953, in the general election, the Progressive Conservative party advocated in the plainest terms an increase in the income tax exemptions to $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married persons. I sought to put the same view forward for the consideration of the Minister of Finance when I spoke in the house on January 24. It is most unfortunate that the C.C.F. in bringing an amendment of that kind, a commendable amendment to that extent, has linked it with a hairbrain proposal to place a tax on capital gains, a proposal which if it were to be put into effect would frighten off capital and do the Canadian economy untold harm.
Canada needs capital. We need capital created out of the savings of the people. That is one reason why the government ought to be making resolute efforts to reduce the burden of taxation on the Canadian people. What other source of Canadian capital is there? If the government is not going to permit the Canadian people to retain more of their earnings in the form of savings, and therefore of capital, then Canada will have to continue to look abroad for sources of needed capital.
I wish to refer to a statement made recently by Mr. Ashforth, president of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, at the annual meeting of that bank, when he said:
Week after week one reads of foreign concerns purchasing Canadian arms or establishing new plants and factories in Canada. The same opportunities are available to Canadians. Why don t we grasp them?
Lack of capital, or perhaps I should say savings, is one factor. In some cases, it reflects greater technical knowledge on the part of the foreign company. In others, it represents the establishment of a manufacturing plant in Canada by a company that is already selling its products in this country. But this is not the whole explanation. Evidence is accumulating that Canadians are not showing enough vision, enterprise and courage in relation to the opportunities open to them.
Risk-taking is essential to a dynamic, expanding economy. In the mining field, Canadians have proven that they are prepared to take risks, and the rewards have been substantial. More of the same enterprise and courage is needed in other sections of the economy.

Let hon. members weigh well those words of Mr. Ashforth, that "lack of capital, or perhaps I should say savings, is one factor" accounting for the unfortunate and regrettable fact that Canadians are not taking advantage of the investment opportunities open to them in the development of Canada's resources.
I have some comments to make on the sales tax. This government proposes to continue the sales tax upon the necessities of life undiminished one whit. Why is it that this government insists upon placing this levy on the necessities of life of the Canadian people? There was a study made recently of the sales tax by the Canadian Tax Foundation. Some interesting facts have emerged from that and other studies. About 58 per cent of sales tax collections are from consumer goods. About 24 per cent are from industrial purchases. Based upon 1954 revenues within the consumer group the largest items subject to this tax were clothing and personal effects. They occupied 15 per cent of the total, or $110 million. We are speaking now of 15 per cent out of total sales tax collections in the neighbourhood of $650 million a year. The sum of $110 million or 15 per cent of the total represented levies upon clothing and personal effects. Another $76 million or 10 per cent of the total was levied upon purchases of household appliances, furniture and furnishings. How can any Minister of Finance justify impositions like these upon consumer necessities? So many of these articles to which I have referred come strictly within the category of necessities for the Canadian family. These impositions are to be continued by the will of this government. There will be no diminution this year. Every hon. member opposite in voting to support these budget proposals expresses his determination to continue these impositions undiminished upon the purchases of necessities by the Canadian people.
The second feature of the sales and excise taxes which is worthy of mention relates to a reduction that was made last year. The government last year actually reduced from 15 to 10 per cent the excise tax levied on automobiles. What was the result, sir? A reduction in revenue? On the contrary, there was an increase in revenue. The collections from the excise tax on automobiles actually exceeded those of the previous year by $8 million. I suggest that there is a lesson there to be learned by the Minister of Finance and by the government. A few more reductions in rate would not necessarily mean serious and crippling reductions in revenues. On the contrary they would assist the circulation of money and the expansion of business enterprise.
The Budget-Mr. Fleming
The third comment I wish to make concerning sales and excise tax relates to the report of the Carter committee. The minister made brief reference to this report in his budget speech a week ago tonight and paid very proper tribute to the worthy public service rendered by the members of this committee. The report itself came into the hands of hon. members only yesterday. That report has been in the hands of the minister and the government for weeks. Why was this important report virtually suppressed until now? I say it is typical of the attitude of the government. The minister had the report and the government had the report. It was obviously a report which required study. But in their view what does the House of Commons matter? Who are these troublesome people who call themselves members of parliament? Why should the government concern itself about such persons? Therefore they have kept the report virtually under lock and key and hon. members were not permitted until yesterday to receive copies of this report. I do not think that does justice either to the House of Commons or to the quality and importance of this report submitted to the government by public-spirited and competent men.
We have a new tax proposed in this budget, sir, a tax on advertising. Let it be understood by all that this is the government's proposal; it is not the proposal of any Canadian publisher. What is the fundamental and underlying purpose of this proposal? Like everything else in the budget it is anything but clear. It has been shrouded in fog just as the whole subject has been shrouded in secrecy until the minister made his announcement a week ago tonight, a secrecy which indeed invites the suspicion of hon. members.
Has the minister made clear the government's objectives in relation to this proposed tax? No, he has not. If the minister had come before the house and said something like this: "Concern has been expressed over the way in which the Canadian market has been deluged with a flood of American magazines and we are concerned that Canadians should be assured of Canadian magazine literature to read, so we are going to take effective steps across the board for this purpose," the situation might have been different. There would have been some rhyme and reason to that. That would have been an understandable objective.
But that is not what the government has done. Without any clear statement as to its purpose the government has chosen in this proposal to place a tax upon a particular type of magazine. It has not applied any form

The Budget-Mr. Fleming of restriction or imposed any burden upon the whole flood of United States magazines that enter the Canadian market and which are bought by interested Canadians in such large numbers. No, the government has chosen rather the discriminatory course of proposing a special tax upon a special group.
We do not like discriminatory taxes. There have been protests already from United States sources and there have been many Canadian protests. As was inevitable, there are some magazines which evidently were not within the thought of the minister when he proposed this tax and which are now pointing out that they are going to be affected by it. They are not among those which were referred to in the press or in the talk that went on around the corridors. Of such are magazines whose chief purpose is such as the dissemination of medical information, magazines edited by competent medical sources.

That is the third year in a row that we have imported more than we have exported. In our trade with the United States, last year we imported $840 million more from the United States than we sold to the United States. That was an increase of 40 per cent over our import surplus in commodity trade with the United States in
1954.
Seventy-three per cent of our imports continue to come from the United States, and just 11 [DOT] 6 per cent from the United Kingdom. Sixty per cent of our exports are going to the United States; only 18 per cent to the United Kingdom. Our imports from the United States last year were up 20 per cent over 1954. The British Prime Minister has been pleading for a transfer of eight per cent of Canadian purchases from other sources to the United Kingdom to balance their trade with us.
We know that in consequence of these results, which have the full approval of the government and are created largely by its own policies, a current account deficit of $665 million was incurred in 1955 as compared with a current account deficit of $431 million in 1954. This deficit was increasing by leaps and bounds in the last quarter of
1955.
These facts and the growing domination of the Canadian economy by United States interests, which were reflected in them, are matters that ought to be engaging the serious concern of all Canadians. I should have liked to enlarge on the subject of economic domination of Canada by United States interests and trade, but I fear I shall have to leave that for another occasion.
Let me say in conclusion that this budget has been properly described in the Conservative amendment as a partisan budget. We have a repetition of the cycle in budgeting. This is the political cycle. We must wait for the year of elections for needed reductions in taxation. Meanwhile the government's policy is to soak the people and ignore their problems. It is the same old mentality so clearly revealed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce: "If we wanted to get away with it, who would stop us?" This government wants to get away with the policy of "soak the people and ignore their problems." It is the build-up for next

year, and one is left with a strong suspicion that there has been an unwarranted underestimate of revenue in this budget in the course of that build-up.
This is a cynical budget, and I say to you in my final words, sir, that this budget, with sickening features about it, as the Winnipeg Free Press has said, reveals the sickness and the infirmity and the decrepitude of this government. This government is suffering in expenditure from elephantiasis; where action is needed, it is suffering, and with it the Canadian people in consequence, from paralysis; to the voice of the Canadian people it is deaf; to its own responsibility to the Canadian people it is blind; and it suffers from a psychosis springing from its own delusions of grandeur, omniscience and infallibility.

Mr. Speaker, we appreciate your consideration in permitting us to be associated with other hon. members in this budget debate. The budget motion and the speech from the throne motion are two of the most important motions that any session of parliament considers. Around the activities involved in the budget and the speech from the throne all of the government revolves. The speech from the throne outlines the government's program and the budget advances its fulfilment. Of the two the budget is the more important because it includes provisions for taxation and the method of financing so that the policies that have been suggested by the government can be made effective. Without the budget the world of government would stop. The wheels would stop going around.
Included in the budget are the millions for health and social welfare all expended in this country, the millions for the dominion-provincial agreements, the millions for the necessary defence expenditures, the millions for national housing, the millions for veterans' benefits, the millions for farm loan operation, the guarantees on loans on wheat, floor prices on butter, hogs and eggs, Agricultural Prices Support Act expenditures, the payment of storage charges on grain, even the policing of the country, the operations of the experimental farms all contained in the budget. Because of the enormous expenditures contained therein and what is involved in the operations of government and the benefits to our people through the budget, I am sure that all parties in the House of Commons are going to support it.
If I were a member of one of the opposition parties I should not like to be in the position of having to go back home and say that I had voted against all these benefits for our

people, that I had voted to defeat the government so that none of these benefits would be possible. I suggest to the leaders of the opposition parties that they give their members a free vote so that they will not be held responsible by their electors and will not be blamed for endeavouring to destroy a government that has raised the national income over and above all expectations of anyone in Canada or anywhere in the world and has contributed to the greatest extent in history to the well-being of all our people.

The reason I did not take part in the wheat loans debate was that I was waiting for the opposition to say something. They made 77 speeches and there was not a word in any of those speeches that I have not heard before and ever since I came to the house in 19491. They were all the same. They were no different from the speeches they made in 1951, 1952, 1953, 1954, and before that. Their speeches were all the same. We Liberals represent the people without continuous repetition and we obtain results. We Liberals do not speak often but when we do speak we convince the people. Why should we speak on opposition motions? Why should we speak on these members' motions? We did not invent them. We did not bring them, with their irresponsibility, before the House of Commons. We did not agree that those who did bring them before the house were representing the same line of thought out in the country that I, at least, represent or think I represent. I was particularly interested in remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more). Not one of my people back home has asked me to vote for a Social Credit motion, resolution or amendment, but my people have told me to be on my guard against certain proposals

The Budget-*-Mr. Studer advanced for political reasons that would destroy the economy that has been built up in this country.
This may not sound just right, Mr. Speaker, but if there is any obection to it you will have to blame it on the fact that I spent a lot of my youth in Iowa pulling weeds out of the cornfields and perhaps that had an influence on me. In any event, back home on the farm there are three tools that we think are indispensable around the farm. One is a pair of pliers, another is a screwdriver and the third is a wrench. We save ourselves a great amount of trouble on the farm by carrying these three tools in our pockets, by tightening up screws if there are any screws loose, by tightening up wire if there are any haywire proposals or anything of that kind around the farm and also by tightening up any nuts that may be loose. My people told me to take these three tools with me to Ottawa because I might be confronted with the same thing down here in connection with some of the proposals that are advocated in the House of Commons.

The people in Saskatchewan are asking me: How much is a weatherbeaten old socialist speech worth? The answer is that it is worth nothing. I think the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) in his constituency is in trouble or the farmers possibly are. The proof that they have no influence, the proof that they are only speaking for 2J per cent of the people is in the fact that they have told us a hundred times in this House of Commons that they were representing the farmers of western Canada in connection with those bank loans to farmers. Therefore I would suggest that they improve their technique, that they either send representatives here that the people of Canada can have confidence in or govern themselves accordingly and tell their people, as they should tell them: We Socialists have not been in a position to obtain any results for you so it is useless to send us back to parliament in Ottawa. My duty is to represent the non-socialist farmers of western Canada. A strange thing has happened in western Canada. X represent the non-socialist farmers. The strange thing that has happened is that all the socialist farmers are now rich farmers. They have accumulated all the land. Every socialist in Saskatchewan and every socialist in this house has bettered his position 100 per cent since he has been here and since this Liberal government has been in existence.
