I appreciate the government assistance we have received of $32 million on account of excess wheat storage. But that amounts to only half a month's wages to the average farmer out in western Canada. So lest anyone think that is the solution to all of our problems, let me say this. Some of the troubles are local but some of them-and we hear this even from the mouths of the socialists-are ungovernable as far as Canada is concerned in the world upon which our economy depends. The most striking thing to all the people of the world is how far Canada has advanced in spite of the abnormal, overwhelming situation where we are dependent on other countries of the world for our very existence through our exports. No country in the world has made a greater contribution in producing things than have the people of Canada, including the farmers. The

The Budget-Mr. Studer first thing we need is that the wheat move into the channels of trade. Nothing should be left undone anywhere by any department of government, the wheat board, the railways or individuals wherever they are connected with the determination of the movement of wheat. Nothing should be left undone to the end that some money will be in the hands of the farmers this coming spring by means of which they may finance their spring operations. Nothing should be left undone to see that the organizations allocate their grain orders to the various elevator companies in Saskatchewan on an equal basis as much as possible so that all can avail themselves of some of the financing, and so that it may be fairly done. Nothing should be left undone. While we are talking about box cars, let me say that some of the socialists try to make political capital out of something which may not be in existence six months from now.
We do not want to forget some of the big things regarding the future of farming in western Canada. I think one of the greatest is the international wheat agreement. I for one sincerely hope that the future will produce an international wheat agreement under which all the countries of the world, including the exporters and the importers, will agree to a price for that wheat that will make it possible for the people of western Canada, and the people of all of Canada, to produce that wheat in unlimited quantities without any shackles placed upon them through any limitations in regard to the establishment of parity prices, which immediately involve controls, not only of acreage but also of the number of farmers. Even some of the wise men of western Canada will agree with that.
Mr. Bobier, vice-president of the wheat pool, in speaking to the select committee of the Saskatchewan legislature a little more than a week ago said that the initial price on wheat of $1.40 at the lakehead works out to about 70 per cent to 75 per cent of parity. He went on to say that if 100 per cent of parity were established they would have to control production to prevent growers from going wild in production. Mr. Hannam, of the Canadian federation of agriculture, had something to say in regard to parity. We all want the equivalent of parity. If it is not called that, it should be. Who should pay the parity? Should it be the consumer, or should it be the people of Canada, including the farmers? After all, if you establish parity you have added not one thing to the national wealth. You merely distribute the wealth that there is in the country. Therefore, I say the international wheat agreement is the most important document that we can ever devise in the whole world. It convinces the consumer that the farmer should have a parity

price, not paid for by himself in his own country but by the individual who consumes the wheat. We are striving for that to increase the national wealth of Canada. That is why it is so important. In my opinion, the important thing is to have the equivalent paid by the people who eat the product. That is what we wish to have in western Canada. We farmers pay a parity price for everything used in production. The consumers throughout the whole world should pay. Eighty per cent of our production goes to the whole world. That is so important. It is important that our representatives over in Europe should continue their negotiations for an international wheat agreement so that the farmers and all the people of Canada may be able to live as they should live and so they may have the equivalent of a parity price structure. If we get that, then we shall be able to continue to feed all the people of the world and we shall be able to continue the vocation that we have adopted as producers for the betterment of mankind.
Mr. Hannam, president of the Canadian federation of agriculture, said that if we adopted parity:
We would lose our United States market for beef and pork.
Incidentally, if we adopted 75 per cent of parity we would find that the prices of all of our products are above that percentage with the exception of rye and beef. Immediately, all these prices would have to come down if we were to establish parity so that they would not be above the 75 per cent.
As Mr. Hannam mentions, it would be impossible to sell our commodities in the United States. He said:
Unless we put on an embargo against United States beef and pork, they would swamp our market.
That, of course, is logical. That is why our hog prices were established at a floor of 23 cents. Mr. Hannam went on to say:
We would compromise our whole case in the eyes of the world-because Canada has been a key supporter of freer trade.
Freer trade has been in existence in Canada because this government has reduced tariffs by nearly 40 per cent in the past decade, and it has continued doing so, and is again doing so in this budget.
Mr. Hannam went on to say:
We could not avoid complete government control and regimentation of agriculture-even to production and acreage controls.
Some hon. members say that they do not believe him, but you cannot deny economics. Mr. Hannam went on to say:
It would lead inevitably I believe, to more regimentation than our Canadian farmers would be willing to accept.

Everyone knows these things. He went on to point out some of the other pitfalls that we would fall into. Everyone knows these things except people who do not study economics. The people who are in that position just pick up discarded policies that have been thrown away throughout the world, policies that were never workable anyway, except through national support such as they have in the United States, which will eventually have to be discarded. There is no possibility of the Canadian people pulling themselves up by their bootstraps to make such a policy workable. That is why all the people of the world have to be convinced of the crying need of the farmers and that we must have a price to enable us to live, if you would care to call it that. They need such a method to make it workable and to make it possible to have a system that is not so complicated that it will defeat itself in the end. Therefore, the government is concentrating on the farmer's position.
One hears much about the national wealth and what we are to do about it. How are we to create a system that will see that all classes get their share of the national wealth? I do not know of anyone who does not think that he is getting less of the national wealth than he is entitled to. I do not know of any particular industry, occupation, or vocation that does not think along that line, human nature being what it is. Everyone thinks that the other person is better off than he is. One thing you can be sure of, and that is that the farmer is going to demand his fair share of the national wealth. Many things are needed in western Canada, but we have gone without them. I have been living on my farm for 40 years. This fall electricity came into my yard for the first time in those 40 years. The socialist government is advancing the policy established by the Liberal government many years ago in setting up a power corporation. We are responsible for putting that pole in my yard, but it cost me $580, and that is a lot of money in any man's country, especially when we are in the position that the socialists say we are in, in western Canada. The Liberals of Manitoba put in electricity for very much less and are charging half as much as we are charged in Saskatchewan for power, but perhaps that will be overcome in a year or so. Also, out in Saskatchewan no farmers are driving Cadillacs. There is not one in a thousand. There are only 12 modern homes in a thousand in southwestern Saskatchewan. Only one farmer in 10,000 in Saskatchewan takes a trip to Florida, and that was one who went because the doctor told him he had to go. Most of our troubles have been on
Private Bills
account of crop failures, and there is no compensation anywhere for lack of crops. There is no one in the world who should have a higher share of the national wealth than the producer. We now have economic commissions all over the country. Every university has its professor of economics. I think we should have a minister of economics in our government. At the same time he could be an economy minister. I think it would be all to the good because you would have someone to co-ordinate matters of production, preservation and distribution, the economy of our country in the future. I think the most important minister in any government in any country would be a minister of economics.

subtopic: PENSION FUND SOCIETY OF THE DOMINION BANK
speechtext: Will the hon. member explain the purpose of this bill?

subtopic: PENSION FUND SOCIETY OF THE DOMINION BANK
speechtext:
The sole and simple purpose of this bill is to change the name of the society from "The Pension Fund Society of the Dominion Bank" to "The Pension Fund Society of the Toronto-Dominion Bank". Although the explanatory notes explain the reason for this desired change of name, it may be useful to give some further information.
The Bank of Toronto and the Dominion Bank were amalgamated under the provisions of the Bank Act and became the Toronto-Dominion Bank, effective February 1, 1955. Both banks had pension funds, that of the Dominion Bank was administered through the pension fund society of the Dominion Bank, and that of the Bank of Toronto through trustees.
Following the bank amalgamation, it was naturally desirable to amalgamate the two pension funds and full authority for this action was contained in a schedule to the amalgamation agreement which, under the

Private Bills
Bank Aet, has the force of law. After full consideration, it was considered that the society was the more convenient vehicle for the amalgamated fund and all necessary steps have been completed to vest the fund of the former Bank of Toronto in the society.
New by-laws governing the amalgamated pension fund have been prepared and approved by the income tax authorities and are in operation as of November 1, 1955. These by-laws, in which the best features of the rules covering the two former pension funds have been incorporated, have been authorized by the board of directors of the Toronto-Dominion Bank. They were also approved and adopted at a special general meeting of the members of the amalgamated fund held at the head office of the bank on Friday, February 17, 1956.
The action of the society in applying for this bill to have its name changed to a name which is now more appropriate to the circumstances was approved at a meeting of the board of directors of the society held on January 25, 1956, and subsequently by a unanimous vote of the special general meeting of the members of the society held on February 17, 1956, referred to above.
This society was incorporated in 1887 by a special act of the parliament of Canada, being chapter 55 of the statutes of that year, and that statute received a minor amendment in 1899 by chapter 112 of the statutes of that year.
Notice of the intention of the society to make application to parliament as above has been advertised in four issues of the Canada Gazette commencing on the 7th day of January, 1956, and is being advertised once per week for four weeks in the Globe and Mail commencing on the 17th day of February, 1956. No indication of any objection on the part of any member of the society or any member of the public has come to the attention of the society or the bank.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, I do not like these finance companies to exist at all. They bleed the Canadian people with interest rates of 24 per cent. I was only pointing out to the house that under a socialist administration arrangements are such that when people must borrow money it can be borrowed and repaid over a reasonable period of years at interest rates of 4 or 5 per cent.
That is a naked lie.

That is the attitude we take towards the needs of the people. I am told that in Alberta the rate is 3J per cent. I think the Saskatchewan government, not having the hundreds of millions of dollars in oil royalties of the Alberta government, on a relative scale has a more favourable rate than the government of Alberta which charges as high as 3J per cent. With the several hundreds of millions of dollars they have they are not sure of what they should be doing.
They are sure.

It has been suggested that we should allow this bill to go through because the people who make up this company should be given equal rights. When something is plaguing me I do not believe in granting equal rights and in welcoming other things of a similar nature to plague me. I do not think the Canadian people would like to see equal rights extended to parasites. We want to see them eliminated. We do not want to see all the people of Canada become victims of this type of racketeering.
I was extremely interested in reading the comments made the other day by the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Richardson), as found on page 2582 of Hansard. I have met him on only a few occasions and I think he is one of the most honourable members of this house. I notice that in his remarks he admits che possibility that the people who have to borrow money from finance companies are unfortunate and I would like to compliment him on that attitude. Since he is a member of the legal profession I assume that he is connected with finance companies only in the process of engaging in his occupation as a lawyer. I do not think of his own volition 67509-169

he would have a hand in these things in any way, shape or form. I gather that from his statement to the effect that he thinks the people who must use these companies are unfortunate. He did say, however, that the majority of the directors of any such companies must be Canadian citizens. He said:
The overriding Loan Companies Act states that the administration of all these companies, including small loans companies, must be only by the board of directors, the majority of whom, as I have said, must be Canadian citizens and residents.
He again comes to the same subject when a little further on he says:
There are to be five directors, the majority of whom will be Canadian citizens and residents.
That is made to sound as if we might after all be dealing with a Canadian firm. I was pleased to find in the same paragraph as the last quotation that the hon. member made a certain admission because I intended to ask him about it. He says:
-may I say that the sponsor of the bill is the Merchants Acceptance Corporation, which has carried on business in the New England states since 1909.
In other words, the hon. member admits that the real owner of the company is this United States organization. I am glad he has supplied us with that information because one of the main issues I intended to raise was that we really do not know who is asking us to authorize the incorporation of this finance company. The hon. member goes on to say:
This indicates that the person, unfortunately if you will, who needs to borrow $100, $150, $200 or $300, can go to this company for such loan on the basis of his personal character and financial integrity as represented by his signature, and as in the case of all of us that would be his warrant for such a loan. That is the explanation of this bill.
I think the hon. member meant to say that that was the explanation for the name that the company has selected. I have no reason to say that the hon. member did not know what he was talking about when he made that statement, but I venture to predict that the Signature Loan and Finance Company, if and when it operates in Canada, will operate much along the lines that other finance companies follow. I have yet to find a finance company in Canada which will lend money on a signature only. They take security in the form of a chattel mortgage or they have the unwritten power to garnishee your wages if you are a wage earner. In the case of a married man all companies insist that the wife as well sign the note. I do not know whether they register these chattel mortgages, but that is their concern. However, I do know that chattel mortgages are widely accepted. I doubt very much the statement that this company is intending to make loans on signatures

only without any other security. The only organizations in Canada that I know of that do that are the credit unions and there are special reasons why they are able to make loans on the basis of signatures only. The hon. member goes on to say, and I quote from page 2583 of Hansard, as follows:
This is not by any manner or means a Liberal measure, a Conservative measure, a Social Credit measure or a C.C.F. measure.
The hon. member is absolutely right when he says that this is not a C.C.F. measure because we intend to oppose this legislation to the best of our ability. I think the hon. member is a little over optimistic in saying that this is not a Liberal measure because when the votes are called I think I can safely predict that there will not be a Liberal member who will vote against this bill. After all, it might be slightly risky for a Liberal member to vote against this bill when it is realized that one of the provisional directors is no less than the president of the National Liberal Federation of Canada. I doubt very much whether any of them are going to have the temerity to so affront their national president.
There is another sentence I should like to consider for a moment, to be found in the same paragraph as the previous quotation. Apparently referring to the Small Loans Act, the hon. member had this to say:
-the act of 1939 invites people to come here and-
I doubt the accuracy of that statement. I do not find any invitation in the Small Loans Act to anyone to come here to do business as a finance company. The Small Loans Act was enabling legislation, it was not an invitation. The existence of such legislation might seem like an invitation to the hungry wolves who would like to prey upon the difficult financial situations into which our citizens sometimes get themselves; but to respectable people, to those who are producers, to those who serve in our society I do not think the existence of the act would be considered an invitation or should be looked upon as an invitation. The concluding sentence in that paragraph reads:
People in all parts of the world are being urged to enter our favourable economic climate, and it is no wonder that they want to come to Canada. They feel that they want to do business here.
This is one type of business that we in Canada can well do without. I do not think the Canadian people are inviting them. I can understand that they may want to do business here because they see the loopholes which the Liberal government has left to permit people being rooked with rates of interest of 24 per cent and more.

When I am asked to endorse the passage of a bill like this I like to look to see who is doing the asking. On looking at the bill I find the names of two citizens of the United States of America, Edward James MacDermott and Charles Thomas MacDermott, Jr., both of the city of Worcester in the state of Massachusetts. I know nothing about these and can only assume that they are the owners of Merchants Acceptance Corporation, to which I referred previously. The hon. member stated that the majority of the board of directors and the management must be Canadians who are resident in Canada, so I find three other names, Duncan Kenneth MacTavish, Ronald Charles Merriam and George Perley-Robert-son. Naturally I wondered who those gentlemen might be. I have been unable to find anything about Ronald Charles Merriam and George Perley-Robertson, except that they are solicitors in the city of Ottawa.
On looking at the latest copy of the Canadian "Who's Who" I find that Duncan Kenneth MacTavish is a citizen of considerable note, and when he asks us for the right to pluck the Canadian people at interest rates of 24 per cent and more I think we should have a look at who he is and see whether he is worthy of the confidence of this house. Reading from page 673 of volume VI, 195254, I find that Duncan Kenneth MacTavish, O.B.E., Q.C., was born in Ottawa, Ontario, 56 years ago, the son of Judge Duncan Byron and Flora. He was educated at Queen's University and graduated from Osgoode Hall Law School and is a partner in the firm of Gowling, MacTavish, Osborne and Henderson. He is secretary and director of Pitney-Bowes Company of Canada Limited; vice-president and director of British American Bank Note Company Limited; director of R. L. Crain Limited; Holden Manufacturing Company Limited; Holt Renfrew and Company Limited; the Southam Company Limited.
I suppose we can expect the Ottawa Citizen, which is owned by the Southam Company, to come out with an editorial saying that parliament ought to pass this bill. He is a director of the Ottawa Valley Trust Company, Wallace Realty Company Limited, Imperial Realty Company Limited and Red Rock of Canada Limited, whatever that is. He is president and director of Ottawa Car and Aircraft Limited; he might have some defence contracts there. He is a director of the Personal Finance Company of Canada. I cannot for the life of me understand why he wants to organize an opposition to his own finance company, but he may be a patriotic citizen and think that a little competition for the Personal Finance Company would be a good thing.

He is on the board of directors of the Associated Screen News Limited. He is a member of the board of governors of Ashbury College and trustee of Queen's University. I suppose that university students would be good clients for this finance company. He is a member of the national capital planning commission. He has been elected president of the National Liberal Federation. I suppose that, if the company will make the fortunes that other finance companies have been making, the donation to the Liberal election fund will be a very handsome one.
He read law with Colonel A. T. Thompson and E. F. Burritt, Ottawa; he was called to the bar of Ontario in 1926 and the bar of British Columbia in 1950. He was made a K.C. in 1937. He is in an organization called Zeta Psi; I do not know what that is. He is a Liberal and he is a Presbyterian. I did not think that Presbyterians allowed any church members to be on the board of directors of a finance company. However, be that as it may, for his recreation he plays golf. He belongs to the Rideau Club, the Country Club and the Royal Ottawa Golf Club. He has a home-incidentally, I do not know when he has time to go home, but he has a home-at Thorold road, Rockcliffe, Ottawa. He has an office at 88 Metcalfe street, Ottawa.
After reading that amazing list, I just wondered what his occupation might be, and so I had to take the supplement. I am rather fussy about these people who receive the right to take out of the pockets of Canadian citizens these exorbitant rates of interest, and therefore I think I should pay some attention to who they are. I find in the directory which is a supplement to this "Who's Who" that among the many occupations he lists himself as being engaged in law. I do not know where this man is going to find time to administer another finance company. I am very suspicious that the two Americans named are the ones who are going to operate this finance company and that any Canadians who might be on the board will be on it only in a very nominal manner in order to comply with the provisions of the act, which says that, out of a board of five, at least three must be Canadian citizens and residents in Canada.
Unlike the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer), who says that the socialists exercise no influence in Canada, I feel that the socialists exercise a tremendous influence. A year ago this whole subject of these finance companies was first raised in this house by the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue). In the issue of Saturday Night for March 17, 1956, there is an article 67509-169i

headed "Tightening Up on Small Loans" by Logan MacLean, which is very well written indeed. He makes the following statement in relation to my argument that not another finance company is needed:
Licensed lenders at the end of 1954 had some $219 million of loans outstanding, including $88 million of less than $500.
We raised the issue last year, and we got such an excellent reception from one end of Canada to the other that this year the minister himself has seen fit to make some moves in the right direction. 1 am not permitted at this time to discuss Bill No. 51. However, when the hon. member says that we serve no useful purpose in our protestations, I want to say that in this instance, with this bill and other bills like it, I think we have served a very useful purpose. The article in Saturday Night shows that the interest rates on $1,200 for 12 months will have been reduced from $156 to $109.50, or a saving of approximately one-third. Taking the figures of the loans outstanding now, I think the C.C.F. is responsible for saving the people of Canada in interest alone, with even the limited measure of reform that we are getting this year, a sum in excess of $1 million each and every year henceforth.
Don't let your imagination run wild.

Someone says not to let my imagination run wild. I might say that, if it were not for the C.C.F. members in this house, the imagination of the many sleeping members of the Liberal party would run very wild indeed.
Oh!

I have said what I want to say, Mr. Speaker. I do feel that the hon. member who has volunteered to be the sponsor of this bill is personally in no way to blame. I feel very resentful that the president of the largest political movement in Canada should associate his name in any active role at all with finance companies, and particularly with the formation of additional leeches on the Canadian people. I want to register my opposition all the way along the line to the formation of another finance company.

Mr. Speaker, this is a motion for second reading of Bill H-5 from the other place, and I understand it is to be referred to the banking and commerce committee. The petitioners whose names are given in the bill, Edward James MacDermott and Charles Thomas MacDer-mott, Jr., both of the city of Worcester in the state of Massachusetts, Duncan Kenneth MacTavish, Ronald Charles Merriam and

Private Bills
George Perley-Robertson, of Ottawa, and others, have brought forth a bill which, as has been explained by the sponsor, is in proper form. In supplicating parliament for incorporation by this method, they are not only following the approved method but are within their rights in every respect. The question is, then, how the matter should properly be dealt with in this house.
The merits of the case, as I see them, should be dealt with after the petitioners have had the opportunity of presenting those merits to the banking and commerce committee. If we were to attempt to prejudge the issue here on second reading and, as has been suggested, defeat what is brought forward in proper form and in accordance with proper rights, then we would in effect be making our decision before hearing the evidence, which I am sure no fair-minded member of the house would wish to do. It would be like what, I am told, has sometimes been done by an inexperienced magistrate. Coming to a conclusion after hearing a plaintiff and being advised that he could hot render his judgment at that time, he heard the defendant and then decided the case in the opposite way. We will have an opportunity, to which I for one will look forward, of hearing these petitioners present their case. I look forward to it because I should like to know what the case is for further use of United States capital in the small loan business in Canada. That is an issue which might be debated but I submit it would probably be better debated after we have heard the purposes advanced by the petitioners. We could, I suppose, spend considerable time debating the whole question of small loans, interest rates and collateral issues that are before parliament in other ways, but that does not strike me as being a useful expenditure of our time at this stage. We could debate the narrower question of whether there are enough companies in the small loans field now, but I submit that would be better debated after we have heard the petitioners.
A bill of this kind is not a government measure but is brought forward in the ordinary course of the rights of a citizen to petition parliament for incorporation, and therefore it seems to me that the only proper course to follow is to let the bill go forward to the banking and commerce committee where we shall hear the petitioners. As I say, I look forward to hearing these particular petitioners because their names and places of residence arouse an interest which I am sure evokes a full inquiry as to the purposes and merits of the proposition which they will then ask parliament to accept.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add my voice to those who have expressed their opposition to the incorporation of another small loans company. I think that in Canada we have had enough of the kind of treatment that forces poor people in unusual circumstances to go to these loan sharks incorporated under charters similar to the one proposed in this legislation which we are now discussing. The first and most lasting education I got in Sunday school comes from something that I recall most vividly, the picture of Jesus driving the moneychangers out of the temple. From biblical times right down to the present day methods have been followed throughout the centuries by which our common people, our little people, have been exploited by another class regardless of whether or not that class was a minority.
Under charters of this type individuals are given the right to prey upon people of this dominion when they are most in need of a better form of assistance. I want to join with others who supported the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) when he first brought before the house a year ago any active opposition to this type of company. Since that time there has been more recognition throughout Canada of the fact that many of our people with small incomes, people who are in the most straitened circumstances, have to go to companies with such charters as the one being sought at this time. While our group may be small, while our influence may not have spread sufficiently throughout Canada to bring about widespread opposition to this sort of thing, I am quite sure it has been effective in moulding public opinion with regard to the fact that a rate of interest of 24 per cent is much too high to charge people at any time but more particularly when they are in dire need. I support the hon. member for Assiniboia and other members of the house, not only of this party, who are prepared to get up and try to bring to the attention of the government that we need a different type of legislation in order to meet the requirement for loans of people who are in dire need.
Contrary to what the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) said earlier this afternoon, in my opinion this party is having a tremendous influence on the thinking of people throughout Canada, and while we do not win every victory we are still prepared to get up and say what we think. I believe that in this instance we have something on which public opinion in Canada should be focused. I am not against any particular company. I am against the principle of anybody having to pay 24 per cent interest

on any type of loan and more particularly when they are in dire circumstances.
By way of argument, I suppose, against the views put forward by the hon. member for Assiniboia and others in the house against the present practice, certain loan companies have undertaken to put up a defence. I have here a little pamphlet issued by the Niagara Finance Company Limited. It is very interesting from the point of view of what they have to say in support of their argument and the methods they follow in making loans to people. In the foreword to the little booklet they say:
Reputable lenders-
They take it upon themselves to say they are reputable. I suppose that is because they have a charter and therefore they feel they are reputable. I do not think that sort of statement would be swallowed by all of us. I do not want to attack them personally but I certainly attack them on the matter of principle. I do not think it is reputable for anybody to demand that poor people pay 24 per cent interest. The foreword has this to say:
Reputable lenders, such as Niagara Finance, have hundreds of unsolicited testimonials that tell the real story of the value of the lender to his community. Sometimes the stories are poignant, sometimes amusing, often they leave us with a real sense of satisfaction.
I suggest that the greatest satisfaction these companies get is from their interest charges. In my opinion the most significant testimonials will come from people who have bought on time, had to go to a loan company to get a short term loan and finally have lost their furniture, their home, their equity in whatever they may have bought. The foreword goes on to say:
On the other hand, our industry has been the target for unjustified criticism by uninformed people who have never felt the need for. nor used, the service provided by companies such as ours.
Again I want to say that I do not think the criticism against this type of lending, launched particularly by members of this group, is unjustified. I question too that the criticism is uninformed. I do not think you need to have been in the position of obtaining a loan from one of these companies in order to understand what the effects are in the case of many of the people who obtain these loans. It is just as silly as to say that you have to be a hen in order to know how to boil an egg. The pamphlet then proceeds to try to describe why people borrow, and I think this is significant. It has this to say:
Frequently, when families are faced with emergencies requiring ready money (illness, accidents, expensive repair bills for cars or homes, taxes, etc.), they find it necessary to reduce payments for such outstanding bills to smaller, more easily handled amounts.

I suggest it is a pretty facetious argument to suggest that if people take their bills, go to one of these loan companies and agree to pay 24 per cent, it will be any easier for them to repay what they owe and take care of their indebtedness. On the contrary, I suggest that such people are perhaps pledging their future to these companies and will be in direr straits than ever. The pamphlet goes on to say:
The unvarnished truth is that people want to keep their credit intact and pay promptly. If they do not pay promptly then there is a penalty exacted from them . . . worry! Doctors in candid moments say it's more harmful than tuberculosis, the common cold or any other infectious or contagious disease.
Again, what a silly argument to make! If there is any worry involved it arises when people find themselves in the position of having to go to one of these companies to obtain a loan as a result of which they know that when they get their pay cheque they are going to have to make a payment month by month on the loan and if they do not pay there will be a severe penalty. They know that they are faced with a situation where they are going to have to pay 24 per cent interest. So rather than being of any assistance to them, again if the doctors' statements are true that worry is one of the worst things facing people, these companies certainly add to that sort of condition.
Here is a very important matter. This company in particular goes out of its way to attack what, in their opinion, is one of the more important types of organization we have in this country, namely the credit union. Here they say:
Credit Unions . . . Such organizations are often formed in large plants, factories, or among social or community groups. They have the advantage of being run by the members, and their administration and other costs are therefore low. They contribute virtually nothing to the public treasury. They have comparatively no taxes to pay. They do not lend to the general public; they exist to serve their own membership. Be careful not to overlook the fact that operations of credit unions must be restricted to groups with close "community of interests". They can offer low rates of charge only because they are tax-free, can use voluntary staff and usually have rent-free or very low-rent accommodation.
Mr. Speaker, I have had some experience with credit unions because in the province of Saskatchewan we have perhaps more than there are in any other province in the Dominion of Canada. I think it would be interesting to the members of this house-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am normally a patient man, as I think are most of the hon. members here. One does not mind remarks that are relevant to the issue. But when we are dealing with

credit unions specifically, is that not getting a little bit far away from this bill that has been presented here?

speechtext: Not at all. I take it that what we have before us now is a motion for the second reading of Bill No. 166 entitled "An act to incorporate Signature Loan and Finance Company". Perhaps the hon. member for Moose Mountain could devote his attention to the motion for second reading of this bill. There is an amendment which has to do with the six months' hoist. The intention of it is to kill the bill. It would seem to me that the hon. member should not discuss an alternative proposal-he aims at killing the bill by the amendment that is before the house-if his remarks are to be relevant.

Mr. Speaker, I was not proposing that this chamber at the present time accept the alternative, but I think there is an alternative. I felt that within the scope of this discussion I might be able to indicate that I felt there is an alternative method of providing short-term loans to people by means of which they would not be required to pay this exorbitant rate of

interest which is charged by the type of company which is asking for incorporation by parliament at this time.
In defence of the credit unions-if they should need any defence-I want to say that we have a community effort on their part, with no usury and no exorbitant interest rate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I suggest to the hon. member that we have already had discussion on this type of loan legislation, during the course of which hon. members have put forward the benefits to be derived from credit unions. That discussion has taken place on a private bill moved by an hon. member of this house and also on a government bill. In that discussion latitude was given. Now that we are dealing with this private bill, it seems to me that we must direct our remarks to the principle of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think I have given the reason for my participation in this debate. It is certainly to register my complete opposition to the bill. I feel that what we are aiding and abetting here, if we allow the incorporation of this company, is just one more small loan company with the privilege of exploiting the hardship and the difficulties that the Canadian people suffer at this time. Rather than that this government or any member of this house should allow such a thing to take place, I think it is expedient that we give consideration to those methods which would give better standards of living to our people. Particularly at this time, when it seems that there is greater and greater need for credit in this country, I think some measure should be found as an alternative. Already this session there have been five bills dealing with increased lending facilities for many classes of the Canadian people. Small loans companies generally do not carry on very much business in my constituency except in one or two of the larger centres. However, I do feel that in protesting against this bill I am speaking for the large cosmopolitan areas where there are slums and where we find many people in the low income brackets are becoming victims of this vicious system. Therefore, I want to protest in the strongest way I can.
Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, a little earlier in the debate the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) spoke of the reference of this measure to the banking and

commerce committee and said on that occasion he was looking forward to seeing and meeting the sponsors of this bill, because, in his words, "their names excited interest". Well, Mr. Speaker, the only sort of interest their names would excite in me would be rather a macabre one.
Sir, perhaps I am old fashioned. I was reared in a different sort of world when we called things by their real names before we became so very delicate as we have become in recent years, so delicate, shall I say, as to call undertakers morticians, and so forth. In the world in which I was brought up money lenders were called money lenders. They were not glossed over as lending institutions, even approved lending institutions, or small loans companies. They were money lenders and no one even pretended that they were respectable members of society. They were considered by all respectable people as being a rather disreputable element in the community. I suggest to you, sir, that if we would continue that practice of calling things by their real names those people might not be deluded into supporting some of the measures that come before us.
I am interested, sir, in the light of the exuberance of the statements of the Minister of Finance that we are in a booming, bouncing economy, to notice the ability that this sort of people show in trying to get into the small loans business, because we had better not close our eyes, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that they are coming in for one purpose and one purpose only, and that is to fatten on misfortune. It is no good the sponsors of this bill pretending that these people are coming in to perform a public service. It is the same sort of service that hyenas and vultures perform; and if there were not in our community a growing number of people who find that their regular sources of income will not pay their regular living expenses, then those people would not be so anxious to get into the field. There would not be the competition to get licences and charters to do business among the unfortunate members of our society, because those people must all be classified as unfortunate. Some of them, of course, may be unfortunate merely in the fact that they are not bright enough to realize that those so euphemistically named organizations are nothing more or less than the old-fashioned money lenders, the sharks. It is unfortunate that they are so unintelligent that they do not realize that. The vast majority, however, are unfortunate in a plainer and more readily understood manner. They are unfortunate in that they do not get enough money to live on. And they are driven at some point or another by some misfortune,

I would myself much rather see the government devoting itself to a more positive cure of this situation, a cure that would ensure that the incomes of the Canadian people were sufficient to meet their living expenses. There are, of course, a number of ways in which that could be done. One would be, perhaps, to curtail some of the incomes that are so cherished by the Minister of Finance and his colleagues and distribute the proceeds in the form of increased family allowances and increased old age pensions. But I do suggest, sir, that to attempt to cure an apparently chronic state of impecuniousness on the part of a vast number of our people by allowing old-fashioned money lenders, sharks, to get into the field with the blessing of this parliament and to fatten on that misfortune is a disastrous policy for this parliament to pursue. I would like to see this parliament very firmly put a stop to any more expansions in this disreputable business, and to take proper steps to eliminate the need of this by additions to the incomes of the ordinary citizens of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock we were discussing a situation in regard to the economy in general and in regard to the farming population in particular. In the 13 minutes or so that are left to me I would like to offer a few more comments and to suggest again that in this economic world in which we live one of the most important folios of any government at this time would be to have a minister of economics. We are living in the age of automation wherein machinery is taking the place of the labour that was formerly involved in the production of goods and services. To have such a portfolio would be advisable and of advantage. I think he would be one of the busiest ministers in our government if a portfolio such as that were to be established.
What are the objectives of this government in regard to farming? Well, the objective is to learn from the experience and the policies of all countries and to determine what has been detrimental or objectionable to the farmers' interests. What this government is trying to do is to eliminate the objectionable features of all other policies in all countries and to utilize the beneficial features that have been incorporated in any existing policy and all the policies throughout the countries of the world which have been of advantage to the farmers.
This government proposes to use the floor price structure, the Agricultural Prices Support Act and subsidies where necessary, and whatever might be beneficial in the parity price structure. The government intends to utilize all these measures and incorporate

them into one overwhelming policy, if I might call it that, which would be greatly beneficial to the farmers of this country. In doing so this government wishes to have the support of all opposition parties and all the people in Canada. Only a government such as this is capable of doing the job. This government has the interests of the farmers at heart and it has the support of all the people of Canada. Only such a government can formulate these policies and make them effective. There is no hope anywhere in a puppet or splinter government or a government that is local or operative in one province or which has only the support of people in various small sections of Canada. We have to have a government which has the support of people throughout Canada in order to make effective the beneficial measures which we hope to bring into effect. These would be of benefit not only to the farmers but to people of all occupations and classes in Canada.
We have had many speeches concerning duties and tariffs. The government is progressively reducing tariffs. It has removed them from machinery and repair parts in this budget; but we farmers will make a deal with this government and with the people of Canada. If they will remove the entire tariff structure which exists in Canada today, then we farmers will not ask for any consideration or subsidies or anything else from this government. We will be prepared to meet competition throughout the whole world. The farmers will be able to produce more in a free economy as opposed to a tariff economy. I think that would be accepted anywhere, Mr. Speaker. As the result of that we could go forward from here and formulate these policies if we have the support of the people.
In connection with a tariff economy I would suggest that the farmers themselves cannot win in a tariff battle because they are overwhelmed with regard to voting strength throughout the country. We do insist, however, that the rest of the people of Canada give consideration to the situation in which the farmers find themselves and eliminate any extra burdens which the farmers may carry through any policy that may be in evidence here in Canada. The problems of farmers never seem to end, but if they ever do end this government will be responsible for ending them. Here again I ask for the support of the Canadian people. All is not lost in Canada. We are more or less in a period of transition wherein we are moving from an agricultural economy to an industrial economy. Perhaps in the over-all picture as a result of increased industrial expansion and increased wealth the farmers can depend for
The Budget-Mr. Studer their subsistence more on that type of economy than they could if we had a depressed economy. It is in the interest of the farmers and of all the people in Canada to have the entire economy come to the assistance of agriculture when that is necessary.
All is not lost in Saskatchewan, either,, because industry is supposed to be coming, into Saskatchewan; at least the premier of Saskatchewan is telling us about it every day.
I think it should because I notice that even the licence plates for Saskatchewan automobiles are made in Manitoba. If industry is. coming into Saskatchewan in the face of the Regina manifesto which reads, "We will not be content until the capitalists have been eradicated," and with that sword of Damocles

how do you pronounce that name, anyway?-hanging over their heads, then a situation must exist in Saskatchewan which is not in evidence anywhere else. If industry is-coming into Saskatchewan under those conditions then there must be a conspiracy between that psuedo-socialist government of Saskatchewan and the capitalists to eradicate not the capitalists but the socialists in Saskatchewan. The socialist government has a. secret alliance with the capitalists to eradicate the socialists in Saskatchewan and the purge is on. It began in Swift Current last fall at a nomination meeting in which the only real1 socialist in the government of Saskatchewan was purged. He did not receive the nomination in Swift Current last fall for the socialist government. My Tory friends are quite vocal here. I would like to suggest to them that they dissociate themselves from the socialists out in Saskatchewan. They have nothing incommon. Their ideals are not only contrary but absolutely contradictory to the ideals of socialism.
There is a saying that politics makes; strange bedfellows and there is nothing stranger than what is taking place out in Saskatchewan. The Conservatives have been in bed with the socialists so often that no one knows to whom the bed now belongs. I would suggest to those Tories that when they get into bed with them, as they do so often; here in this house, they pull down the shades; and pull the sheets over their heads so people cannot see who they are.
The Karl Marx juniors on the left side should get up and stipulate what is going, on out in Saskatchewan and they should, state whether or not they are socialists.

speechtext:
I would be glad to do so, Mr. Speaker, but I thought they would be proud of it. All we are interested in is hearing some real down-to-earth, honest-to-goodness socialist speeches in the House of Commons. No wonder the president of the socialists in Saskatchewan, who is a teacher of English socialism in the University of Saskatchewan, Carlyle King, was pleading with the socialists to please make a socialist speech so the people of this country will know what you are and whether you are socialists or merely capitalists in disguise. Hon. members to my left frequently ask the Liberals to make speeches. We are all looking forward with pleasure, as are all the people of Canada, to hearing these hon. members make socialist speeches so the people of Canada can determine what they are.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that this is a good budget. It ensures progress for Canada, in which we are all in-;erested. It ensures benefits to all of the people. Nowhere in any country are there greater social services; nowhere in any country has a system been devised where we can produce to a greater extent. Nowhere in any country are there greater exporters. Nowhere in any country is there greater leadership. Where is there a greater country? Where is there a greater future? Which all adds up to this: There is no substitute for good government, there is no alternative for good government. This government has proved in the past, in the present and will in the future, that there is no end to good government.
