speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, this afternoon the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) referred to the budget as a do-nothing budget and he said he was opposed to it, but it seems that about six o'clock his wife presented him with twin daughters and I think he should be congratulated.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in all the accounts that have been written or spoken about the budget presented a week ago I cannot find where anybody, even friends of the government, has said that it is a good budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said it was.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There were many things in it, but the most significant thing to me is that it has been accepted by everybody as being a formal government announcement that there will be no election this year. I think this is a feature which even the most ardent supporters of the government will deplore. The reason for the no-election assumption is obvious. For many years now we have had an election budget in every election year and it has been taken for granted that the long-term strategy of the government is to manipulate the taxes of Canadians to suit the purposes of the party in power. It does not matter how callous we may become to this sort of thing, it does not matter how it may be justified even in some minds as practical politics, I am sure that it does not increase anybody's respect for the government or the law of the land, and the budget is a part of that law.
If next year is to be an election year then I suppose we will have an election budget again. There is disheartening evidence in the figures placed before the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) that there has been deliberately built up this year a surplus of revenue to provide funds for the political purposes of the party in power in the next election year. The Minister of Finance gave recognition to this surplus in his remarks to the house a week ago tonight. He excused it by pleading that it made sense in good times to budget for such a surplus. However, he made no reference to the fact that this excuse is completely opposed to the budget policies and pronouncements of recent good years.
Apart altogether from the callous acceptance of partisan demands as the basis for budget decisions by this government, there are other factors which tend to make this deliberate government practice entirely reprehensible to many Canadians. Some years ago this sort of thing might have been excused as good political sport, but times have changed. The money which the government is now jockeying around from election to election represents

one-fifth more or less of the entire productivity of all the people of Canada. What the government does about this one-fifth of our money from year to year vitally affects the whole course of the economic development of this nation. Under the present government this tax grab, to use a common phrase, has been acknowledged as part of the relentless policy of centralized government control. Taxes which were once regarded only in the light of necessary government revenue are now openly manipulated at the will of the government to force the current doctrines of the ruling economic group in Ottawa upon the nation. This use of the taxing power, developed during war emergencies, may have had some temporary justification, but it seems to me that its extension into normal times has led inevitably into its extension into the realm of party politics. Surely this is going beyond the best judgment and the best conscience of what our people expect from their national government.
There are serious drawbacks to the general economy, and by that I mean the future of Canadian development, in this hard-fisted and hard-boiled approach to budget decisions. For one thing, the economic theories of the ruling group are not entirely consistent from year to year. The result is that the planning of businessmen become subject to annual guessing about which page of what theorist the Ottawa group happens to be studying.
For some time we have been told that this government believes in free trade with a capital F and a capital T. We have read some rather funny, but certainly very positive, statements by representatives of the government at meetings of GATT and in lectures to spokesmen for the textiles and other industries who have come to Ottawa suggesting that there are times and occasions when this belief in free trade at all costs might be modified when this or that Canadian industry finds itself in serious trouble.
We will all recall the insults which were thrown at the representatives of the textile and other industries who were told in no uncertain terms that they would not be asking for protection if their own industrial management was as efficient as the Ottawa theorists thought it should be. There were many Canadians who did not agree that this all-out free trade position made much sense in the light of the facts of international marketing, but most people I think gave the government a measure of credit for what appeared to be a sincere if misguided adherence to a rather odd economic theory.
The new budget removes even that belief in the sincerity of the government in this matter. It includes what I am told is the
The Budget-Mr. Starr most complete reversal of form in the whole history of government dabbling in economic theories. I refer to the drastic measure of protection now offered to the magazine industry. Without going into the merits or demerits of the specific industry concerned, some generalities are obvious.
First, this is protection in the most drastic form. It is a tax designed to penalize the non-domestic sector of an industry in order to divert revenues to the domestic industry. I do not say that this is necessarily a bad principle, especially if it can be shown that a Canadian industry could not survive without this protection.
Second, the nature of the tax makes it a form of censorship. Its purpose is clearly to influence the type of publication which Canadians are to read. It is a clear-cut infringement of both free trade and a free press.
Third, it is the very worst sort of public relations that a young, expanding country can have. It labels Canadians in the eyes of our most important customers abroad as being small-minded parochial people who are afraid of the import of ideas, particularly American ideas. It makes a complete mockery of the huge expenditures by the government's tourist department who are trying to persuade Americans that they are welcome here in Canada.
I mention these aspects of this extraordinary tax, not to attack it as such but rather to point out the amazing about-face of the government on the whole question of protection. It has denied protection, in very high-sounding and self-righteous terms, to industries that needed protection far more than the thriving magazine industry. It may be of interest to note also, for example, that the current issue of the Financial Post, which carries an account of the budget, also carries an article headlined "Magazines Increase Ad. Sales". It states that Canadian magazines sold $17-4 million worth of advertising last year, which was an increase of more than $1-3 million over the previous year. That is an increase of 7 [DOT] 6 per cent in revenue.
In spite of this fact, the Minister of Finance had this to say about his amazing excursion into the field of protection:
The long-run continuation of Canadian magazines appears to be jeopardy.
I cannot believe that the minister meant that seriously. The facts of the matter are that the long-run continuation of Canadian magazines is not in any jeopardy whatsoever. We have Canadian magazines that have achieved circulations and revenues in recent years that are far greater than ever before in the history of this industry. They have

The Budget-Mr. Starr done so because they are good magazines, well edited, efficiently run and giving the Canadian people what they want to read.
The minister, in spite of the facts of the situation, says that what he calls very exceptional measures can be justified. How can these measures be justified? The facts are all to the contrary. Industries which have been steadily losing sales have been denied relief for years. Now, one which is increasing its revenues is given a degree of protection- a 20 per cent levy on revenues-which is unmatched for severity in the recent history of protective taxation.
I have no brief for or against Canadian magazines. I read and enjoy several of them, both in the general field and in special trade fields in which I am interested. They are doing a fine job. Two of them, Weekend Magazine of Montreal and the Star Weekly of Toronto, have in recent years developed national circulations of about a million each. No United States magazine has done so well comparatively in its own field in this period. This is not a depressed Canadian industry. On the contrary, it is a thriving, prosperous example of Canadian enterprise at its competitive best.
Yet we have this industry drastically protected. Why? The minister suggests that the decision has something to do with preserving Canadian culture. That is a laudable objective. Will the government, then, protect private Canadian radio stations against United States owned radio programs which are being brought into Canada by its own agent, the C.B.C., and which in turn are diverting advertising revenues from Canadian radio stations? Will it tax the Canadian editions of the New York Times and the Times of London, which are also owned abroad but are diverting advertising revenue from Canadian newspapers? Will it tax United States and British movies which are now diverting advertising revenues from other Canadian media? Surely it would be logical to do so, if there were any logic whatsoever in this bombshell of an excursion of the government into high protective tariff legislation.
Many Canadian businessmen are disturbed about the effects of the inconsistency of this action on foreign investment in Canada. Surely the owners of United States magazines who have invested heavily in Canadian editions were entitled to believe that our government was sincere when it said its policy was international free trade. Their investments were based on good faith in our word. How much faith can they, or any other United States businessmen, have henceforth in the declared policies of any Canadian government?
TMr. Starr.]

I do not like to impute motives. I am more willing to believe that this protective tariff venture is rather a budget "boner", attributable to the credulity of the minister, than a form of special protection for the government's propaganda machine. I sincerely hope that the minister and his advisers will be able to excuse it in this light. The alternative viewpoint strikes too deeply at the roots of political decency to be tenable even by a political opponent of the government.
Yet, no matter how we view this amazing about-face on free trade, it cannot be fairly considered without reference to the things the budget did not do. The spectacular nature of the one invites speculation about the others. The long-outmoded luxury taxes are left unchanged, in spite of the evidence of the figures placed before this house by the minister that some of these taxes could have been reduced without the loss of a single cent in revenue to the government. Two specific cases will explain just what I mean.
A year ago there was a reduction in the automobile luxury tax from 15 per cent to ten per cent. The minister at that time informed this house that this would cost the federal treasury in the neighbourhood of $26 million. The figures he gave the house two weeks ago show that the actual result has been a gain of $8 million to the treasury.
The cigarette tax is another example. I read the brief of the tobacco growers on this matter. It was supported by the expert opinion of leading economist's. It showed that excessive taxes had cost the industry and the treasury millions of dollars. It also proved, citing facts and figures from the government's own estimates, that the tax reductions of 1953 and 1954 had increased federal revenues and that a reduction this year would do the same. It is easy to say, of course, that this is only the opinion of the growers, but the facts are that for several years now the growers have been right and the Department of Finance has been wrong.
These are but two examples. With them in mind, surely it is reasonable, even for a layman, to wonder if there are other taxes which are being held at high levels for no other reason than that the Department of Finance, having built them up as a result of wartime patriotism, now refuses to reduce them, regardless of facts, regardless of fairness, and regardless of their limiting effect on the growth of our Canadian economy. The great Chief Justice Marshall of the United States once said that the power to tax is the power to destroy. In a lesser degree, but too often forgotten, it is also the power to harass, restrict and bedevil the normal growth of a national economy.

There is no evidence whatsoever in the budget of a realistic examination of the tax structure in the light of the basic needs of our whole Canadian economy. Such an examination is regarded by the majority of our leading economists and businessmen as long overdue. But no such examination appears to be within the remotest realm of possibility, under the present government or the present regime in the ministry of finance. This year it could not be done because it was not an election year. Next year it will not be done because budget changes will have to be related to the political requirements of a forthcoming election.
I am not, Mr. Speaker, privileged to speak for any political party. But I do say that there are those on this side of the house who are close enough to the Canadian wage earner and consumer and who have some knowledge of business, even if it is not big business, to promise that when we sit over there we will raise our voices and use what influence we have to see that the whole Canadian tax structure is taken out of politics and placed where it belongs, in the realm of economic realism in regard to the future of Canadian enterprise, progress and expansion.
I appreciate the difficulties which confronted the Minister of Finance this year. I appreciate even more the difficulties which will confront him next year. The minister will have to prove himself a political and fiscal miracle worker to match the election year budgets of his illustrious predecessor who gave the Canadian people the two largest tax reduction budgets in the history of Canada in the last two federal election years, namely, 1949 and 1953. They were the only two budgets in history to top the $300 million mark in tax reductions. No non-election year budget has ever been that generous.
In the years between elections we have had a different story. It has been the rule rather than the exception to add new or increase old taxes in non-election years and to remove or decrease them in election years. It is not surprising that the items which figure most prominently in this kind of manipulation are those which make an immediate impact on voters. The pattern is so clearly established, Mr. Speaker, that I venture to offer the minister a tried and true formula for his next budget. It is solidly based on the political sagacity of his predecessor. I cannot offer it at this time as the platform or even as the suggestion of any group or party in the house, so, for want of a better name, I offer it to the minister merely as Mike Starr's 1957 budget suggestions.
First, there will be reduction of personal income taxes by an average of 15 per cent in
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher the lower and middle brackets and an increase in exemptions from $1,000 to $2,000 and $2,000 to $3,000. Second, there will be repeal of the 10 per cent luxury tax on automobiles and all other personal and household items to which special excise taxes have been added since 1939. Third, there will be a decrease in the tax on cigarettes from the present $1.77 per carton of 200 to about $1, substantially cutting the 100 per cent which the government now adds to the cost. Fourth, there will be removal of the present limitations on the deduction of medical expenses from income tax. Fifth, there will be removal of the remaining taxes on soft drinks, candies and other small pleasures of children.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that the suggestions I have just made will prove helpful to the minister next year. I make them at this time because we have often been told that the minister and his advisers start to work on the new budget just as soon as the current one has been placed before the house. I have not detailed the total cost to the treasury of these tax changes, but a rough total makes it clear that the funds are already in hand or on the way. That, in fact, appears to be the outstanding feature of the budget now before the house. It is nothing but a delayed action budget.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year it was my privilege to vote for the first budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). I regret very much that I cannot do the same on this occasion. Despite the well-meaning of the minister, despite his very good intentions, I feel obliged to say that this budget is a dangerous document which should cause every Canadian, and particularly every Liberal, to stop, look and listen. The high rate of Canadian taxation which has been gradually and insidiously built into our budgets since world war II is like a malignant cancer. For a few years the effects may not be apparent, but unless treated the ultimate result is inevitable.
The government professes to believe in the free enterprise system. Yet I say tonight that it is undermining that system by high taxation, just as effectively as any socialist government could do by decree. When the history of this period is written it will record that one of the great mistakes of the Liberal party after world war II was its steady and consistent failure to give a real measure of tax relief to the Canadian people.
In his budget speech of 1955 the Minister of Finance said this, as found at page 2732 of Hansard of April 5, 1955:
I am sure that all will agree that when employment and incomes are high, and the economy

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher expanding at a normally healthy rate, we should fully balance our budget, with a modest amount for the reduction of debt.
During the past year we had the greatest volume of business, we had relatively full employment, we had the highest national income in our history, and yet the Minister of Finance has given us not a surplus but a deficit. He has given us not debt reduction but debt increase. In so doing he has violated the sound budgetary principles which he himself enunciated 12 months ago.
In the coming fiscal year the Minister of Finance is proposing to take from the pockets of Canadian taxpayers the staggering sum of $4,755 million. That is an increase of almost $390 million over a year ago. Spending on this scale is without precedent in peacetime. To make a comparison one must go back to the critical years of the war, at a time when the federal government was engaged in a fight for survival.
The increased spending this year is not concerned primarily with defence spending. It is concerned with civilian departments right down the line. 1 do not think it is necessary for me tonight to remind hon. members that governments at all levels are taking today about 33 cents out of every dollar earned by the average Canadian. Nor do I have to remind the house that the standard rate of corporation taxation after certain basic exemptions is still 47 per cent.
The question which must confront parliament tonight is simply this. Can we afford to divert such a large proportion of our labour and industry to government, at a time when the country needs so much capital for its growth and development? You cannot spend a dollar of production twice. If the government is going to spend it, then individuals and business cannot do likewise. When we pay out the fruits of our production to defend countries richer and more populous than Canada, when we sell butter to the communists at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer, when we pay out millions of dollars in non-productive subsidies, let us realize that this money is not going to be available for private enterprise to develop Canada.
I have heard a good deal of criticism this session, Mr. Speaker, about the degree to which United States capital is coming into our country. Some people find it strange that we apparently need the Americans to help us finance the trans-Canada pipe line. But is it any wonder that this capital is needed when our government takes from Canadian companies almost half their earnings, which otherwise would be available for reinvestment?
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is a school of thought which contends that high

taxes need not necessarily affect prosperity. In support of that theory they point out that since the war we have had very high taxation, and yet instead of having a slump we have had booming economic conditions. But surely this is a dangerous conclusion. Our prosperity since the war has been caused by a number of unique factors which may or may not continue. I cite the great inflation of prices which has taken place since 1945, including export prices. I mention technical improvements and scientific progress. I cite the great growth of the United States market and of the United States population as well as our own growth through immigration and natural increase. I mention the great resources which we have discovered since 1945. All those factors have combined to give us prosperous times. As a result of those factors the Canadian gross national product increased from $11-8 billion in 1945 to $26-6 billion during the past year. That is roughly a 2 J times increase. The federal tax base, of course, increased roughly in the same proportion. Thus it has been possible for the federal government to finance greatly increased expenditures by simply appropriating a share of the rising physical production of the nation which constitutes a sort of surplus or windfall.
I think it is more than conceivable that the favourable circumstances which we have had since 1945 may not continue. A decline in national product, increased foreign competition, recession in the United States, widespread unemployment-any of those factors- could work havoc with our tax structure.
During world war II and during the Korean war, Canadian tax levels were sharply increased. But, with the end of each emergency, the voracious appetite of federal spending departments continued. Indeed in some cases it was increased. New demands and new programs rapidly devoured the sums of money which formerly had been spent on the war effort, and which might have been used for tax reduction. As a result, the level of federal government spending as a percentage of the national income has steadily risen for the past generation. In 1929 that percentage was 6-7 per cent; in 1947, after the war, it was 17-05 per cent but in 1954 it was 22-06 per cent. This budget continues that 11 year trend despite booming economic conditions.
I suggest to hon. members that there is a limit to the money which you can take from an individual without impairing his ability to keep himself solvent and to save a proportion of his earnings. I believe this limit in peacetime has been reached, and for that reason I contend the budget is a dangerous document.

The great tragedy of the present situation, as I see it, is that no one is very greatly concerned about it. Anyone who suggests that governments perhaps are spending too much money is considered to be old fashioned, antisocial or reactionary.
I blame the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) tonight for not combating more firmly demands for increased expenditures. He above all must realize that there are some things which may be socially desirable and which are even financially possible in this great Canada of ours, but which nevertheless, in the long run, may be economically risky or even suicidal. I recognize the fact that the Minister of Finance has great pressures put upon him, and I do not blame him completely for the present situation.
I will say quite frankly that we in the opposition must bear a good deal of the responsibility for the present ominous level of taxation in Canada. Already this session the C.C.F. group has proposed resolutions which, if passed, would have cost the taxpayer several billions of dollars. In his budget speech, the leader of the C.C.F. group advocated larger old age pensions and a health scheme more comprehensive than the one which is being contemplated. Yet at the same time in his amendment he proposed that the sales tax and income taxes be reduced.
Many people expect such motions from the C.C.F. group. But they do not expect motions and resolutions of the same nature from the Conservative party. Most people expect financial responsibility from the Conservative group. Yet with all respect I must say that from this far corner of the house it sometimes appears to me as though that responsibility is lacking. Maybe I am biased, but far too often it seems to me that the Conservative party proposes policies which seem designed primarily to show the nation that they can surpass the Liberals and even the socialists in their ability to spend the taxpayer's dollar.
I should like to cite only one example. I recall a motion moved several weeks ago by the Conservative group, which proposed Canadian parity prices for agricultural products. That was a proposal which would have been fantastic in its cost, and its success, in my opinion, would have been dubious. The Conservative premier of Ontario, Mr. Frost, recently called on the federal government on the one hand to embark on a nation-wide health scheme and, on the other hand, to give the province of Ontario another $100 million. For my part, I find it difficult to find such proposals consistent with traditional Conservative policy.
The demands of our provincial governments are not very helpful to our federal government in keeping down our tax level.
The Budget-Mr. Thatcher
This year the federal government is proposing to transfer to the provinces in special grants $384 million. Incidentally I may say that I think the figure is about $34 million more than they transferred last year. I think most people in all parties are sympathetic to the principle of these transfer payments. Yet I view with alarm the steady efforts of our provincial governments on the one hand to demand greater expenditures from the federal government, and on the other hand simultaneously to demand that federal authority absorb more of their provincial costs.
I think that such efforts are based on a fallacy, an illusion that if a province can hand over its tax burden to the federal authorities in some way the inhabitants of that province will escape from them. It seems to me that the people who pay federal and provincial taxes are the same. No provincial government should think that Ottawa is a kind of fairy godmother. It is the duty of the Minister of Finance to tell the provincial governments that for the time being at least parliament has reached the limit.
I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that I am sometimes concerned over the attitude of many individual Canadians towards high taxes. I am sometimes concerned over the apathy with which they view the subject. Today most of our citizens watch their personal finances fairly carefully. They do not make a purchase unless they are sure that they are getting value for their money. Their attitude toward government spending is usually different. In Canada today there are many hard-headed and intelligent people who see nothing wrong with the oft-repeated phrase that "government will pay half the cost". There is a tendency to forget that the government's income is money that it takes from every citizen in the land. As one finance minister said, there is no magic in government finance; before you can give a dollar to one person, you must take away that dollar from someone else.
Unfortunately governments today are criticized far more often because they are spending too little than because they are spending too much. There has been little desire for economy in public spending among most Canadians. There are some individuals who feel that because they are in the lower income groups they are escaping federal taxation. That idea is fostered by certain politicians who glibly suggest that huge spending programs can be financed simply by "soaking the rich". Nothing could be farther from the truth because, unfortunately, there are not enough rich people in Canada.
I should like to refer hon. members for a moment to a publication put out by the

The Budget-Mr. Thatcher Department of National Revenue and entitled "Taxation Statistics, 1955". Actually it applies to the year 1953. On page 27 one finds that 4,682,420 Canadians made out income tax forms in that year, and yet on page 35 one finds that out of that huge number only 28,220 had incomes of more than $15,000. In other words, 99-4 per cent of all Canadians earn less than $15,000 a year.
Again on page 35 of the same publication [DOT]one finds that the amount theoretically obtainable by confiscating all income over $15,-000, after allowing for standard income exemptions, is $673 million; but since the government was already taking $233 million from those tax brackets, the net proceeds from total confiscation would be only $440 million, [DOT]or 9-3 per cent of our current budget.
Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, any way you look at it, it is the average Canadian, the working man, the white collar worker, the professional groups, the farmers, who are paying the large proportion of income tax in Canada today, and it is very important that they should realize this fact.
Because the taxes are so often collected as a deduction from the pay envelope, the worker never sees the money and so he is not too concerned about the matter. I think the same can be said about most of our hidden taxes. Ninety-nine out of every 100 Canadians pay such taxes as the 10 per cent sales tax, the 15 per cent luxury tax on television sets, custom duties, tariffs, excise duties of all kinds, in blissful ignorance of the amount which is being siphoned off to the federal treasury. I say that no matter how the budget is planned, no matter who the Minister of Finance might be, it is the average working man who is paying federal taxes. Whether it is corporation tax passed on in the cost of goods, whether it is hidden taxes which are also passed on in the cost of goods, or whether it is income tax, the little man pays.
I believe, and I believe this very sincerely, that if the government went back to the old way of collecting income tax, and took it from the taxpayer in one lump sum on April 30, people would realize the extent of federal levies. I would also like to see the government put all hidden taxes itemized on the purchase tag, so that people would realize the amount of these taxes. If such action were taken I would venture to say that within a year we would have some action on our budget, because there would be a very vigorous protest, a very loud outcry, right across the nation.
Apart from the attitude of individuals, apart from the attitude of the provinces, apart from the attitude of members of this house,

I think that our present tax levels are caused by two main factors: first, defence; second, social welfare. I have neither the competence nor the time to deal with defence tonight, but I should like to say a few words about our social welfare program. I am one of those who believe that Canada, with its vast resources and with its wealth, should steadily strive for better social services in all fields. But I also think that our country must proceed gradually within the bounds of economic capacity and national solvency.
At the present time the federal government is spending on social services $1,060 million. Within a year, as I understand it, we are going to embark on a new hospitalization program. We are told that the cost of that program will be $180 million for the federal government and $180 million for the provinces. If the experience of Saskatchewan and British Columbia is repeated, I suggest tonight that the cost of that scheme will be very substantially more than the figure we have been given. How far can such measures be extended within the framework of national solvency and growth? Already this session we have listened to many resolutions on social welfare. Many new expenditures have been proposed by hon. members. I should like to mention only three. First, there was the proposal to increase family allowances, which would cost $200 million. There was a proposal to increase old age pensions to $60 a month at a cost of $450 million. There was a proposal to extend the proposed hospital scheme to make it into a complete medical-dental scheme. That would cost $600 million. Since there is already a budgetary deficit, such measures could only be financed out of straight taxation increases. That would mean as usual, that the Canadian citizen would have to bear the cost from his hard work and toil.
I hope that in the years to come it will be possible for Canada to legislate for such reforms. But I am convinced that for the time being, the country is carrying a peak load of taxation. Any new advances in the 'field must await further economic development throughout the nation, or a sharp decrease in defence expenditures.
Today we are faced with a number of examples of the dire effects of overloading an economy. It has been said repeatedly by many eminent authorities that the British economy is moving from crisis to crisis, and that Britain's welfare state program lies at the heart of her economic difficulties. The economies of France and Italy are also suffering from a similar sort of social overloading. With these examples before us, Canadians would do well tonight to stop, look and think.

Here in parliament irresponsible motions made in connection with social welfare measures, which overlook economic facts and realities, serve only to arouse false hopes and bitterness. There is a real danger to the nation when any political party, using the taxpayer's own dollar, recklessly endeavours to buy political favour by outbidding other parties in the social benefits it will pay. Mr. Speaker, I strongly believe that in the next few years the government must resist further major demands for increased federal expenditures; rather, it should consolidate and strengthen its taxation base. Such action is necessary for the economic health and prosperity of our nation.
I believe that the minister's fiscal policy in 1956 should endeavour to do the following things. First, it should halt rising government expenditures. Second, it should take more aggressive action to eliminate waste, duplication and extravagance in government spending. Third, it should use the major portion of the government's share of any growth in the national product for tax reduction. Fourth, it should modify the tax laws and encourage thrift and initiative. Mr. Speaker, I believe that failure to follow such policies will ultimately mean that parliament will be forced to pay all its federal bills in the easy coin of inflation. Surely, such a result should be avoided.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I am a comparatively new member in the house I do not intend tonight to go into the ands, ifs and buts of the budget. I will say, however, that if one says too much at this time about the budget it will be like locking the door after the horse is stolen.
First of all, I should like to say it has been my privilege to travel across the length and breadth of this country twice in the last year. In doing so, I have been able to get more or less a rounded-out picture of what Canada is really like and what the people across this nation have to put up with in some of the provinces, what some of their problems are financially and otherwise and to get a general picture of Canadian life and economy. Naturally we are all interested in our nation but I think we are all more particularly interested in our own area, riding or province. The speeches on the floor of the house throughout the year bear that out, I think, and I am no different from other hon. members who have spoken. Tonight I would like to review some of the progress that has been made in the northern area of British Columbia known as Cariboo riding. I focus attention tonight on Cariboo riding for one particular reason and that is because it has had a tremendous growth in the last few years
The Budget-Mr. Leboe and it is still growing rapidly. I might say that the rest of British Columbia is also growing rapidly but the growth in Cariboo riding has been spectacular over the last couple of years.
Perhaps I should say now that my purpose in making a comparison between what the government survey has shown in the past years and what has actually taken place has to do with the position of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway in the development of that northern area.
Hon. members will realize, of course, that the riding of Cariboo is perhaps the largest riding in Canada, being 950 miles long and 350 miles wide. It covers an area of approximately one-third of the province of British Columbia. There is a great deal of developing to do in this area and it is already well under way.
First of all I would like to take you into the northern part of the province to the Skeena riding just outside the Cariboo riding a short distance from Lower Post in the lower area close to the Yukon boundary where we have what is known as the Cassiar asbestos development. The known reserves of this development in 1954 were some seven million tons of asbestos. Today the tonnage of asbestos is being shipped out along the Alaska highway some 300 miles by truck and then over the railway to the coast and on down to Vancouver.
When the Pacific Great Eastern Railway is pushed into the northern area within 200 miles of Fort Nelson I can visualize that the distance from railhead, without the transferring of the goods, will entice the tonnage coming from the Cassiar mines into the lap of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway freight business. It is going to mean a lot to the whole northern area once the railway is projected as far north as Fort St. John. Fort Nelson has an army headquarters and a good airport and a population in one area of approximately four or five hundred people, with three or four hundred people in another section. It is an important and active little town.
As we look around the area of Fort Nelson we find there are some 500,000 acres of arable land which could be used for agriculture and there are vast volumes of timber in the valleys that stretch forth in every direction. All this development is there waiting for proper transportation. We find that in the northern part of British Columbia, as in many other parts of northern Canada, it becomes a matter of long distances. The distance from Dawson Creek to Lower Post, for instance, is 600 miles; to Fort Nelson, 300 miles, along the Alaska highway.

The Budget-Mr. Leboe
The Alaska highway is costing the federal government a great deal of money in maintenance each year. I would like to say at this point that I think it would be well for the federal government to look into the possibility of paving at least a portion of that highway in order to save maintenance costs. The gravel which is now on the highway is working down into the mud and the base of the road and it is not very long before a complete reconstruction job will have to be done on many parts of the highway. I know this to be true because I recently travelled over a great section of that highway.
Coming further south from Fort Nelson to Fort St. John, which has a population of approximately 2,500 people, we find that in the Fort St. John district there is a terrific agricultural development. There are many thousands of acres, and perhaps I should say millions of acres, which have yet to be brought under cultivation in that area. I believe the total arable land is around 3,500,000 acres in the Peace river area and a great portion of that is in the Fort St. John district. A great deal of the grain that is shipped from Dawson Creek at this particular time, which makes Dawson Creek the largest grain shipping point in the British commonwealth, comes from the Fort St. John area. This, coupled with the great forested areas around Fort St. John, points up the fact that there is a great deal to be gained by bringing into Fort St. John the Pacific Great Eastern Railway with its outlet to the coast. This means that when the railway comes north of Fort St. John it will literally be in the front yards of many sawmill operations in that area. It will mean more money in the pockets of the farmers, the people who are working in the lumber industry and those people engaged in the exploration for oil and gas.
It was my privilege to be in Fort St. John at the time when the first British Columbia gas was turned on in the grid of the village of Fort St. John, the first town in the province to use British Columbia gas. We now find that the beginning of the west coast transmission line which will run from Fort St. John through Pine Pass and Prince George into Huntingdon and into the Pacific northwest of the United States, with a branch line into Vancouver, has its head in Fort St. John at the beginning of the pipe line. In the construction and the development that has taken place there it is necessary for the producers of gas to put in a scrubbing plant at Taylor Flats and they are now looking for
2,000	men to go to work on this project at Taylor Flats to take the by-products out of the gas before it is put into the gas pipe line. A great deal of the right of way of


the gas line has already been cleared and the pipe is being brought in from Great Britain, shipped up over the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and transported by truck and the northern freight ways into Dawson Creek and on up to Fort St. John.
At this point I would like to say that the purchase of this pipe from Great Britain falls in line with a provincial policy under which we seek to buy goods from Great Britain so that we may in turn sell to Great Britain the products of the forests, fish and fruit. It has stimulated a great deal of business for the province of British Columbia and has brought about active trade with Great Britain.
While I am on that subject I might say that locomotives, steel rails, angle bars and so on for the Canadian Pacific railway also come from Great Britain, while we in turn send them lumber, fish, fruit and other products.
At Hudson Hope there are large deposits of excellent coal. Perhaps I should not say too much about coal at this stage as in most parts of the Canadian economy it seems to be a drug on the market, but I believe the time is not too far distant when considerable power will be developed by the use of coal in high pressure water tube boilers with the steam being utilized in large turbines. We find this process being used in Alberta and I understand it is quite economical. I think the time will certainly come when great quantities of coal will be used in this way.
Dawson Creek, which is located near the Alberta border, has a population of around 6,000, whereas 20 years ago there were only 100 people there. Of course Dawson Creek is famous for its great Scottish pipe band, which is known to all Scotsmen in the country. Dawson Creek is the end of steel of the Northern Alberta railway which comes in from Edmonton and it is also mile zero on what is known as the Alaska highway. Dawson Creek is the junction of two highways, the one coming up from Edmonton and the other coming up from Vancouver through Prince George which is known as the Hart highway.
With the Northern Alberta railway and these highways that are coming through, and also the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, Dawson Creek is going to grow by leaps and bounds. The village commissioners are going to have their hands full in servicing the necessary areas to provide for dwellings and so on. The Dawson Creek airport was too close to the town and it has been surveyed into lots which are being sold for dwellings and the commissioners now have the problem of digging up a new airport site.

It will be seen that the expansion that has taken place in this part of the country is beyond description. I referred to the paving of the Alaska highway and I should like to note that the distance from Dawson Creek to Fort St. John is about 50 miles and certainly that piece of highway should be paved.
Dawson Creek is faced with other local problems. In 1952 or 1953 they got a new phone system, but today that is proving to be entirely inadequate. There are 1,000 people on the waiting list and it takes from 15 to 20 minutes or even longer to get central. The four girls on the switchboard do not know what to do about the calls coming in. The Department of Transport, which is responsible for communications in that area, is putting in a new phone system this fall which will take care of all immediate and future needs of Dawson Creek.
There is another thing that worries the people of Dawson Creek. It seems that it is taking the federal government as long to build one little public building in Dawson Creek as it is going to take the province of British Columbia to build a railroad with two branch lines into the Peace river country. I do not think that that should be. I have been here since 1953 and there was an item in the estimates for a public building at Dawson Creek before I came here. That item is still in the estimates and except for a few plans that is as far as it has gone. I understand that the plans are not yet off the drawing board, that the architects have not released them so that bids can be called. There should be a little more action in connection with some of these things. If the provincial government can build a railroad into the Peace river country, if they can do the surveying and everything else, surely the federal government can build a little old post office building in Dawson Creek in the same length of time.
Dawson Creek has an oil refinery at the present time, and I understand that another one will be put in this spring. There are some defence installations there which add to the importance of communications. All along the Hart highway and the new route of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and along the gas line going south there is a great deal of what we call ribbon development. Little Prairie is the new junction of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, where the branch line goes off to Dawson Creek from the main line going up to Fort St. John and on north. It will be seen that wherever there is a junction on the railroad there is generally considerable growth, particularly when it is located in a good agricultural area like this.
The Budget-Mr. Leboe
Coming on further through the Rockies through Pine pass we find at the Parsnip river crossing there will be a great lumber industry in the near future. The Pas Lumber Company have made application for a forest management licence in that area and I understand it is their intention to put in a pulp mill as well as a mill for the production of lumber.
As many hon. members know, Prince George is ideally located on the Canadian National Railways northern main line running from Red Pass through to Prince Rupert. The population of Prince George is around
12,000	and it is growing as it were by leaps and bounds. I notice from a report in a local paper that building permits are expected to total 6 million next year. The provincial government is building a government building in Prince George which will cost $1,500,000.
Prince George is a great distribution centre, being located as it is almost in the centre of the province. It will be second only to Vancouver as a distribution centre. It is located where the old Cariboo highway joins the Hart highway and is a continuing link with highway 97 which goes through to California. The traffic on this highway extending as it does from California to Alaska is out of all reason considering the population in the area because of the many tourists and truckers passing through from all parts of the country on their way to Alaska and the Yukon.
I should like to mention one or two things with regard to the growth of Prince George. Once the gas line comes in there, there will undoubtedly be many secondary industries attracted to that area. There will likely be a brick factory, and undoubtedly there will be a cement factory somewhere between Prince George and Dawson Creek, because apparently the rock is suitable for the manufacture of cement and some people are already interested in this development. Prince George is the white spruce capital of North America. It ships enough spruce lumber out in one year to build a city the size of Edmonton today. An average of 60 carloads leaves the Prince George sidings alone every day of the year; and that is a lot of lumber. That does not take into consideration the amount of lumber that is shipped from other points, such as Sinclair Mills and Penny and all the other points where fairly large sawmills are located. All this development points to the success of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and the wisdom of the provincial government in extending that railway into the Peace river area.

The Budget-Mr. hehoe
Eighty miles south in the Cariboo riding we have the village of Quesnel, another village of 6,000 or more people. Here we have the one and only private plant in that interior part of the province. Western Plywoods have a plant there, and they put out many millions of feet of lumber and plywood during each year.
When the gas pipe line comes through there, we will have an upsurge in the development of this area in secondary industries also. We have in the area of Quesnel large quan-tites of diatomaceous earth which, I understand, are now being developed. When the gas goes through, it can be used for heating purposes to dry this diatomaceous earth. I understand it is expected to create quite an industry there in that business of getting these products out to such cities as Vancouver. I believe that Calgary is another of the markets where they expect to sell a great deal of this diatomaceous earth.
All these add up to one thing, as far as I am concerned, at this moment, and that is the necessity for realizing that communications are the gateway to development. I do not think that a country such as Canada or a province such as British Columbia should ever wait for the development to take place first and then build the railways and communications afterwards. I believe that the way to open up a country is to create the highways and railways that are necessary, and the country will then open up and develop.
The village of Quesnel also serves Wells and Barkerville. The town of Wells, of course, has gold mines-I believe they are under one management-which produce, I believe, about 1,600 ounces of gold each month. I understand that in the days of the famous gold rush of Barkerville there were actually millions of tons of gravel that were turned over by shovel. The village of Barkerville, which has 50 people now, had
25,000	people at one time. However, I believe there is a historical value in the village of Barkerville which should not be overlooked. It is my understanding that the provincial government is going to vote, or has voted, some money for the restoration of some of the buildings in that area.
I understand that the power from the natural gas, if it is converted to power, would be in the neighbourhood of 10 million horsepower, which is a lot of power. I understand that it is expected that the advent of gas is going to do a great deal towards solving the controversy that has been in existence: fish versus power. We are looking forward to great co-operation there among the federal government, the provincial government and the municipalities in connection
IMr. Leboe.l

with the preserving of the fishing industry and yet getting cheap power for the secondary industries.
Now I turn to the question of federal aid for the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. Hon. members will recall that on 3rd June, 1955, the Prime Minister announced that $25,000 would be allotted to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway for construction of 50 miles. At the same time the Minister of Transport mentioned a very much larger subsidy for another railroad in eastern Canada, of which the first instalment would be as large as the total amount to be spent on the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. The Prime Minister, on 20th of January 1956, made the statement that he did not see that there was any growth in the Peace river area that would warrant a change in the position that they had taken.
I made it my business to find out exactly on what the government based its opinion. I placed some questions on the order paper to find out exactly on what these opinions were based, so that I could judge whether or not it was worth following this thing any further, and as a result I have come up with the following information.
I placed a question on the order paper as follows:
1.	Has the federal government made any economic surveys of the British Columbia-Alberta section of the Peace river area within the last ten years?
2.	If so, when and who made these surveys?
The following answer came back from the Department of Agriculture:
1 and 2. Economics division, Department of Agriculture made the following economic surveys: (a) High Prairie area in 1951. (b) Wanham-Spirit River area in Alberta and adjoining area in British Columbia in 1953. (c) Fort Vermilion area 1953.
In looking into the surveys that were made, I find that one soil survey took in 120 farms. One survey took in 60 farms to find out how the farmers were getting along and how much everything cost them. At Fort Vermilion 26 sections of land were looked at. The area concerned was east and north of Grande Prairie in Alberta. Those were the three surveys upon which the federal government apparently based its opinions. I wanted to find out if there was anything I could get in regard to the shipments of products from Hines Creek and Dawson Creek for the year 1946 to the last year for which figures are available. I asked the following question:
1.	What was the total tonnage hauled by the Northern Alberta railways to and from Hines Creek and Dawson Creek for the years 1946 to the last year figures are available?
2.	What was the freight revenue from these points for the same years?

The answer I received was as follows:
1 and 2. The Northern Alberta Railway Company is jointly owned by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and is not an agency of the Crown. Information relating to its internal operations is not furnished to the Department of Transport. Following inquiries, the dominion bureau of statistics advises that it has no record of tonnages or revenues as between particular points.
Now, I have found out what the reports were. I have them here and I have looked at them. I find that the federal government had absolutely nothing on which to base an opinion. I would suggest that possibly this would be a good time for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to take an unofficial holiday of two or three weeks, tour that great north country, see what is going on there, and then come back and advise the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to what actually is taking place there. In view of the taxation structure that exists I feel we are justified in asking for more assistance than has been offered. As a matter of fact, I think a great deal more assistance is justified under the tax structure we have today.
I realize it has been said that you cannot take money from here or there without getting it from the taxpayers, but there is such a thing as a redistribution of funds which are the result of favourable tax fields. No one can deny that the development taking place in British Columbia has created for the people of Canada a very favourable tax field. It is my understanding that out of the total tax revenue in the province of British Columbia the province gets 15 cents out of every dollar and the federal government gets 85 cents. Therefore I think we are justified in asking for additional consideration to what has been given, especially in view of the reports I have put on the record tonight as to what the government had in the way of information on which to base an opinion.
I am not going to say very much about the budget but I should like to put on the record a comparison of the highlights of the federal budget and the budget of the province of British Columbia. In the Gazette of March 21 there is an article headed "Budget At a Glance", a Canadian Press dispatch which reads as follows:
Finance minister Harris read his budget speech predicting a 1956-57 surplus of $113 million compared with a 1955-56 deficit of $51,700,000. There will be no changes in personal and corporation income taxes. Revenue loss from tax changes, mostly in additional exemptions from the 10 per cent sales tax assessed at manufacturers' levels, totals $12 million.
Canadian editions of foreign magazines containing some Canadian advertising will be taxed 20 per cent of gross advertising revenue starting January 1, 1957. Effective immediately, purchases
The Budget-Mr. Weselak of gold for export for safekeeping may be made without restriction. Total 1956-57 revenue is estimated at $4,763 million and expenditures at $4,650 million.
The Prince George Citizen of February 2, 1956 has the budget highlights for the province of British Columbia. Here they are:
1.	Amusement tax-cut from 15 to 10 per cent and earmarked for hospital construction.
2.	Pensioners to receive $5 a month more.
3.	Civil servants to receive pay increases of between 4 and 12 per cent.
4.	Aid to local government boosted by a total of $2,137,931.
5.	Capital works program of $80,109,000; $37,480,000 for arterial roads and bridges, forest development, roads and mining roads.
6.	Agriculture department to spend 45 per cent more.
7.	Education funds up $3,950,000.
8.	Total budget of $258,427,024 record for province.
9.	Net debt of province reduced 13-50 per capita in last year.
10.	Hospital insurance costs up $1,552,710.
I think these figures speak for themselves. I realize, of course, that the Minister of Finance has to work within the framework of the policy laid down by the government. However, in passing I should like to say that when we are considering the taxpayer the fundamental thing we are confronted with in any budget or any plans we have for the future of Canada is the distribution of the goods that we produce. If we fail to distribute the goods that we produce we can stand up in the house and talk till doomsday about the great production that we have. If the financial policy of the government is not such that the Minister of Finance can work within that framework and cause distribution of the production of the country to be made, then the financial policy has failed and not the Minister of Finance. I believe with all my heart that the fault lies not with the Minister of Finance, who has to work within the framework of a policy, but with the policy of the federal government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering the debate on the budget I cannot help but reflect on the budget debate of 1955 when members of the opposition referred to the budget of that year as delightful optimism, as unsound and as an Alice in Wonderland proposition which had been put before the house. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) was accused at that time of giving free vent to his imagination and his budget forecast of a gross national product of between $25J billion and $26 billion was assailed and for all practical purposes ridiculed. In addition, statements and inferences were made to the effect that budgetary deficits would accrue possibly to the extent of $400 million to $500 million.
What has happened in fact, Mr. Speaker? The gross national product has not only

The Budget-Mr. Weselak reached $25J billion, has not only reached $26 billion but has reached $26-6 billion, an all-time high in Canadian history. What has happened to the forecast of deficits? A deficit was planned by the minister of $160 million and in fact the deficit has been reduced to $52 million.
What has happened to the economic recession predicted by the opposition before and during the last budget debate? The white paper shows that the volume of nonagricultural output rose more than 7 per cent, mining output by about 16 per cent, the construction industry 12 per cent, manufacturing 7 per cent, wages and salaries 7 per cent, investment income by one-fifth, and corporation profits to a level 7 per cent above the previous high of 1951. Net farm incomes as distinguished from net cash income rose by over one-third from the previous year but nevertheless remained 14 per cent below the level of 1953, indicating that agriculture has not recovered to the extent that other sectors of the economy have succeeded in doing.
Employment in 1955 was higher than in 1954 and total employment rose by 2J per cent. This was the economic recession predicted last session by the Conservative-socialist opposition. It is no wonder that the financial critic of the official opposition had no desire to discuss the budget when it was brought down but preferred to devote his time to an examination of the estimates.
Returning to the budget itself, may I congratulate the minister upon his sensible approach to the problem. The Conservative-socialist opposition may attribute to him certain ulterior motives and have described the budget as a preview of an election budget. They have also stated that tax reductions could have been made and would have been made had an election been pending.
I presume, Mr. Speaker, it is characteristic of members in opposition to ascribe motives to any action on the part of the government and to ascribe such motives as will suit their own ends. As a result we can therefore assume that any reference to the budget by opposition members will be such as to place it in its worst light. I do not suggest that we on the government side of the house are totally unbiased, but I do say in respect of this budget that Liberals are on solid ground in giving it their support and recording approval of the government's action in this regard.
Hon. members will recall that substantial reductions were incorporated in the 1955 budget and that a deficit of $160 million was forecast. Hon. members will also recall that in April of 1955 we had experienced an unusual winter of unemployment and that the

graph of economic activity had shown a decline which had been carried over from 1954. Under the circumstances the government was justified in budgeting for a deficit to give what impetus it could to the economy by increasing the amount of money available for consumer spending and to encourage investment.
When the white paper was tabled in the House of Commons prior to the budget, press reaction-and, as a matter of fact, my own reaction-was to the effect that little could be done in the matter of tax reduction by the responsible minister. Anyone who has had anything to do with governmental budgetary accounts knows full well that a moderate surplus, whenever possible, is certainly desirable in order to provide against overestimates of tax revenues and unforeseen contingencies. Surpluses also provide a source for strengthening the cash position of the government. A surplus of 2J per cent as provided in the present budget is certainly not unreasonable, and I would agree with the minister when he describes it as a prudent surplus.
The net estimated surplus for 1956-57 in the budget is $125 million. In 1957-58 it is estimated that payments to the provinces will be increased by $110 million.
The national health plan is expected to cost the federal treasury an additional $180 million. Grain storage cost as well as costs under the Agricultural Prices Support Act-

The blessings of an economy operating at a high level are pleasant indeed to a minister of finance but they bring with them new responsibilities for all of us. A certain responsible daily in my own province, whose opinions I often respect, has referred to the budget as not merely a stand-pat budget but a negative budget, and this has been echoed in the Conservative amendment before the house. With this statement I would take issue and propose to do so. The budget, like any other thing within this confused world of ours, is a relative thing and must be judged in the light of the circumstances which affect and surround it.
The positive aspects of the budget are to be found not only in the printed words of the budget but also in what was not said by the minister when the budget was presented to this house. In the printed word we find certain tax and tariff relief to our hard-pressed farmers. Last summer there was criticism in the west of a tariff board ruling which had resulted in certain farm implement parts becoming liable for import duties and sales tax. Government policy has been in the past that parts like the machinery and equipment itself should enter Canada duty free and be exempt from sales tax. The action in this budget on the part of the government to reword the acts in such a way as to restore duty-free entry to these items and of adding further items to the exempt list in accordance with recognized government policy will be welcomed by the farmers of Canada, and will be of some help to them in combating rising costs. The effect of these provisions is to reduce the cost of these items by about 30 per cent which is not an insignificant figure. The removal of sales tax on certain industrial equipment and building materials will also be welcomed by those affected.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This natural resources policy he is reported to have declared was a point on which there was a sharp and clearly defined division between the Conservative party and the Liberal party.
Western Canadians are not as gullible as the Leader of the Opposition may assume them to be, as the Conservative party has found out. I should like to compare this statement of Conservative policy with that enunciated by Mr. R. B. Bennett, on behalf of the Conservatives at the imperial conference of 1930 when he said this. I quote from page 277 of "Colonial and Imperial Conferences", volume III:
The Conservative party of Canada believes in, and employs, the principle of protection of the home producer of agricultural and fabricated products from harmful interference by world competitors. But it is not part of our policy to exclude from our markets foreign goods, so long as their importation does not threaten a reduction in the high standard of living which our citizens enjoy. On the other hand, it is our declared policy to provide for the consumer a cheap market by stimulating the growth of competing domestic industries to that point of development where they will be able in fair competition with others beyond our dominion, to offer to the Canadian public products of like quality and at prices comparable to those prevailing in the larger markets of other countries . . .
In pursuance of this policy, and to meet an economic situation, brought about by world and domestic causes (it is not necessary here to determine their relative responsibility) the parliament of Canada at a session called for the purpose in September of this year, enacted certain changes in the tariff, designed, in our view, to strengthen the position of the home producer. Certain measures were taken as part of this emergency legislation, to avoid the exploitation of the consumer; and in the good faith and good sense of the Canadian producers we have the necessary assurance of their rigid adherence to these measures.
As a result of the adoption of these protective policies the average ad valorem rate of duty on dutiable imports was increased from the 1929 level of 24-4 per cent to 30 per cent in 1932, and on total imports in the same period from 15-9 per cent to 19-1 per cent.
By midsummer of 1932, Mr. Bennett had found that his policy was not working to the advantage of Canada and in his statement to the imperial conference held at Ottawa in

July of 1932, he had this to say to the conference, and I quote from page 397 of the same volume:
In the past, Canada's manufactured products have enjoyed a measure of protection, though at times it is claimed by some a not wholly adequate measure of protection, in the home market. Our natural products have enjoyed little or no fiscal advantage over our foreign competitors in empire markets. It is now our hope to secure it for them. In as much as the ideal application of the principle of protection involves an equalization of benefits thereunder as between manufactured and natural products, it is the desire of this government to effect that equalization and to find a way for our exporters into empire markets by giving the exporters from these markets a way into ours.
Then, he went on to say:
I have said, before, and I do not desire to minimize the fact, that Canada must have greater export markets for its natural products. No country can live unto itself in this complex age, and with our relatively small population, with our vast and varied natural resources, with our immense exportable surplus in natural products, we perhaps above all other countries must be assured of other markets than our own.
Mr. Bennett, in so doing, recognized the importance of our export markets for raw and natural products and stated that secondary industry must support his proposals, and expressed the belief that they could not but share in the great advantage which will accrue to the exporters of natural products, and also recognized that if our exporters were to have a market we must give to the exporters of these countries a way into ours.
The tariff and trade policy of the Liberal government in 1937, and the same words apply today to the present government, were enunciated by the then prime minister, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, at the imperial conference of 1937, when he had this to say:
The international situation will be reviewed in detail at later sessions. I shall, therefore, not make any reference to it at this point, beyond expressing our firm conviction that enduring peace cannot be achieved without economic appeasement, that political tension will not lessen without abatement of the policies of economic nationalism and economic imperialism. The countries here represented have, I feel, a definite responsibility to join with other countries willing to co-operate in a concerted effort to avoid increasing tariffs or exchange or quota controls, and to lessen, in every practicable way, the barriers to international trade.
In Canada we have endeavoured to open the channels of trade. Negotiations with the United States, and more recently with the United Kingdom, led to substantial reductions in our tariff rates.
The effect of the trade policy stated by Mr. Bennett in 1930 and that adopted by the Conservative party in 1956 is a statement of policy which had then, and now would have, the effect of restricting our primary industries that are uneconomic. Such a policy would undoubtedly suit some people, but from the point of view of the country as a whole it

is the development of Canada's great primary resources that provide, and must continue to provide, the basis of our prosperity and the prime impulse to the expansion of secondary industry rather than government interference.
Our secondary industries are coming and will come naturally and economically, but to push them artificially by limiting primary development is to limit what we can do best and most profitably. The fact that our secondary industries are coming along is indicated by the fact that the index of manufactured production of durables in 1939 was 108. In 1954 it was 297, and in 1955 it was 324.
The orderly expansion which has taken place in both our primary industries and secondary industries, which have pretty well kept pace with each other, should not, I submit, be interfered with by government action. Secondary industries are being established in Canada and will be established where the economic climate of the country or the area permit their economic development. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the only result of government artificially pushing the expansion of secondary industry in order to process all raw materials at home would be the abandonment of the high standard of living which we currently enjoy.
The effect of such a program would be, first, the loss of our foreign markets for agricultural products, mineral production and certain industrial production. We have been reminded by Great Britain and other countries that trade is a two-way street and that unless the way is open for trade in both directions trade will suffer. Loss of our foreign markets will leave only the Canadian market available for such production rather than world markets.
Second, to compete in the export trade such industries would be faced with the problem of competing with industries in other countries where wage production and material costs are much lower. To meet this competition we would have to pay wages, at say, the German level, or perhaps curtail our social security program so as to cut the cost of the finished product by the amount of taxation saved; or make other unpopular adjustments in our way of living, all aimed at reducing the cost of the finished product, thereby reducing the benefits we now receive from selling raw and semi-raw commodities.
Third, if we were not to reduce the cost of the finished product by one of the means I have suggested, and compete with foreign production, these industries, uneconomic by nature, encouraged by government to establish themselves in this country, would have every right to come back to the same government and demand either subsidies or 67509-170
The Budget-Mr. Weselak protection, with the result that the primary producer would not only have lost their markets but the cost of the things which they require would rise, and the cost price squeeze now complained of by them would reach the point of strangulation.
Fourth, the restriction of the development of our primary industries, which would be bound to result from such a policy, would result in the economic development of the four western provinces and the maritimes being slowed down to a level where their only market would be their own local market and that of the central provinces. The development of forest and mineral resources in Manitoba has resulted in a substantial increase in industrial development within that province and has seen the establishment of many industries in the greater Winnipeg area. Similar developments have taken place in Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. These developments have followed as a result of the expansion of the primary industries in these areas which in turn have created a demand not only for labour but for material, and have thus provided a market for local industry within the area itself. This has had the effect of strengthening our provincial economies, which certainly is in the national interest.
I can see nothing, Mr. Speaker, in the Conservative policy of maximum processing of raw materials within Canada which differs substantially from Mr. Bennett's isolationist tariff policies of 1930.
In contrast, the attitude of the Liberal party and of the government has been to encourage international trade and of the two I submit that this is the sounder policy. In 1932, when Conservative policies had gone into effect, these duties were increased on dutiable imports to 30 per cent, and on total imports to 19-1 per cent. They were subsequently reduced by a reversal of Conservative policies by the subsequent Liberal policies to 18-1 per cent, or a reduction of 40 per cent.

speechtext:
What has been done under the federal health grants program toward the control of tuberculosis in Canada in the way of:	(a) providing better

Answer by: Mr. Martin:
(a)	Funds provided by the federal health grants program are playing an important part in stimulating and maintaining the fight against tuberculosis. Increased emphasis on early diagnosis and expanded facilities directed toward early case-finding have proven to be some of the most striking developments since the inception of the federal health grants program. These improvements have occurred particularly through the expansion of clinic facilities, the extension of mass surveys and the introduction of the general hospital admission X-ray program. X-ray equipment, films, fees for interpreting the films taken, mobile vans and other clinic equipment and the assistance toward the employment of additional clinic personnel have

Since 1948, more than $3,390,000 has been made available to the provinces to provide streptomycin, P.A.S., isoniazid and other antimicrobials free of charge to all sanatoria patients requiring them. subtopic: BOOK CENSORSHIP
BOOK CENSORSHIP
speechtext:
1.	What are the titles of each book banned or prohibited entry into Canada by the Department of National Revenue in 1955?
2.	Which of said books was prohibited because of
(a)	its treasonable or seditious nature; (b) its immoral or indecent character?
3.	What officials made the examination of each of the said books, and who made the final decision to ban or prohibit in each case?
4.	(a) Are such officials given special training to qualify them to decide what is proper, from a literary, moral or political standpoint, for Canadians to read; (b) If so, what is the nature of such training?
Answer by: Mr. McCann:
1.	It has been the continued policy of successive governments to not make public the titles of books classified as immoral, indecent or seditious under tariff item 1201 which has been in the tariff since confederation. It has obviously not been felt that the government should be the supplier of a list of selected works of this character. Furthermore, the publication of such titles could serve as a catalogue for those interested in the clandestine importation, distribution or sale of this kind of merchandise. When a publication is classified under this item the importer and the publisher are both personally advised of its classification and have the right of appeal to the tariff board or, with the approval of the minister, adjudication by the exchequer court, li the hon. gentleman asking this question wishes to have a list of the books classified under this tariff item during the year 1955, I will be glad to make it available to him for such use as he may see fit.
2.	The 140 books referred to in No. 1 above were all prohibited as being immoral and/or indecent in character.
3.	Publications are reviewed for purposes of tariff item 1201 by various departmental officers, but the final decision to classify a publication under this item is, as a matter of policy, assumed by the minister, who takes the responsibility before parliament. Depending on the nature of the publication different reviewers are selected within the department and in some cases outside opinions are also obtained.
4.	There are no known courses given in Canada for the purpose of qualifying persons to decide what is proper from a literary, immoral or political standpoint. Where immorality or indecency has to be weighed against literary, scientific or political values in a publication, every effort is made to weigh such values in the method described in No. 3 above.

CHEESE IMPORTS
speechtext:
1.	What are the characteristics of the Garry No. 27 oat?
2.	How many bushels of registered certified seed was grown in 1955 in Canada?
3.	How is this seed obtained at present?
4.	Has any of this seed been exported?
5.	If so, to what countries and what quantity to each?
Answer by: Mr. Gardiner:
1.	The Garry 27 oat is a high yielding variety of medium early maturity well adapted to oat growing areas of Canada. It is resistant to Victoria blight and crown rust and highly resistant to stem rust and loose and covered smuts.
2.	Up to February 29, 1956, 104,655 bushels of Garry seed oats were graded by inspectors of the Department of Agriculture as registered and 264,427 bushels as certified, all produced from crops grown in Canada in 1955.
3.	Seed may be procured from seed growers or seed dealers. Information with respect to seed growers producing Garry seed oats may be obtained from the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, P.O. box 548, Ottawa, Ont.
